A very fashionable Leghorn hat looks well trimmed with a scarf of black hese, which is bordered with creamy duchesse lace, and is hand- somely embroidered at the ends. Above this appear two black and two white ostrich tips, and under the brim at the back there is a cluster of deep yellow roses. This model can also be made with a white scarf, with creamy lace appliqua, or entirely in black, with roses of any colour under the brim.

White serge is not a material which can be recommended for its durability ; still, if an extra gown can be afforded, it certainly makes an ideal seaside costume for a young girl. Strappings of coloured cloth—biscuit, heliotrope, green or red are favourite colours—are largely used for the adornment of such gowns this season, but these additions must be made with discretion, or the result is apt to be showy and vulgar.

AN URGENT CAS.—Patient: "If you don't get me well, doctor, you are likely to lose your fees." Doctor: "How's that ? " "I haven't enough money to pay both you and the undertaker." "Joint, will you get up and light the fire?" "Maria, don't keep making incendiary speeches." "h must be such pleasure to sing as you do. , Does your husband sing too?" "Well, John— John wants to sing awfully and he does." WADLEY : "Awful bother cutting the leaves of a magazine, isn't it ? " Wagrow "Not for me. When I take a magazine home I put it in a con- spicuous place, and some one invariably does the job for me." "OH, we had the loveliest arrangement at our church society last week! Every woman con- tributed to the missionary cause £5, which she ; earned herself by hard work." "How did you get It yours?" "From my husband." "I shouldn't call that earning it yourself by hard work." "You don't know my husband." DEALER—" Here's a cyclometer I can recom- mend. It is positively accurate; not at all like some cyclometers which register two miles, per- haps, where you have only ridden one." Young Lady—" You haven't any of that kind, have you?" DANGEROUS FOR DONKIES.—A traveller having to pass along a very dangerous road in the moun- tain took a donkey driver with him for a guide. On reaching a very steep precipice, the latter said to the traveller—" Yer honour must be very care- ful now, for I've lost many a donkey down there." "I wish, mamma," says little Johnny Fizzletop, ' "that I lived in South Africa." "Why, my son, do you wish to live in South Africa?" "Why, the mammas down there don't wear any slippers." "Yes, my son, but you must also remember that !little boys in South Africa don't wear any pants

For the promenade gown nothing is more useful nor in better taste than one or other of the many fine black woollen stuffs now in vogue. Of course a coloured gown is gayer, but it is certainly not more fashionable, and, moreover, there are few light tints that will stand seaside air and sunshine with impunity.

A black voile, for instance, might have both skirt and bodice tucked—the tacks running round the figure and being arranged in groups of three— and the pouched fronts of the latter, turned back with black silk revers edged with chiffon ruching, from a vest of white chiffon or embroidered muslin. The sleeves should be tucked to match the rest of the gown. The skirt of such a dress could, of course, be worn with blouses, and so made " a double debt to pay."

A STORY is told of a certain estimable dame who says she dotes on " literature " and has a critical taste. Somebody spoke in her presence of Sherlock Holmes. "I do so like Sherlock Holmes," said the somebody; "I was heartbroken when he died." "Oh, so was I," exclaimed Mrs. Malaprop, "his 'Autocrat of the Breakfast Table' has always been my favourite work.' HOURS ON THE FARM. —" SO you didn't like working for old Grumble?" "No ,• worked twenty-five hours a-day." "How could you do that? There are only twenty-four." -4 Oh, well, we kept getting up an hour earlier each day. Why, we did this so regularly that every month we'd find ourselves back into the previoUs day. Great scheme to gain time." AGED HUSBAND "You are going to ruin me with your extravagance. You don't need that cape any more than a cat needs two tails. How often have I told you never to buy anything because it is cheap?" Young wife (with the air of one who has got the better of the argument) : "But it was not cheap; it cost 10 guineas." FEEDING AT FOOTBALL —Seen Leamington Ground, match between Blackburn Rovers and Vale of Leven. Husband—" This Osborn would make a grand man if they would only feed him." Wife (astonished)—" What a shame ! Do they not give him plenty to eat?" SPLENDID COALS. —A coalmaster had just sunk a pit on what he considered a good seam of coal, but to satisfy himself asked an old farmer, who had given the coals a trial, how he was pleased with them, "Oh, rate wed," was the reply. "After burning them all night, we tak' them oot i' the morning and build steno dykes wi' them." THE Texas man who killed a notorious confidence man in New York for not handing over the counterfeit money he had paid for says "He tried to rob me and I laid him out. There has been nothing quite equal to this since the gambler, who, finding that somebody had stolen the extra aces he had tucked into his boots, cried out: "There's cheating going on around this board." "DOES Shacknasty Johnson live near hear ? " "No." " Well, do you know where he can be found? " " No." " bear me! I must have lost my way. Can you tell me where Mr. William 'loon, familiarly known Old Grizzly Bill,' lives, then?" "I reckon so." "Where is it?" "Right yere. I'm Hoon." " Indeed ? Why, they told me at the settlement that Johnson lived within gun-shot of you." "He did; that's the reason he hain't here now." A CLERGYMAN was swindled by a party of horse- copers. When he discovered the fraud, he took the useless horse back to the inn where he had purchased it. Of cource the swindlers had decamped, and the landlord of the inn explained to him:"Well, sir, anyone could see that the men were copers, and I precious soon got rid of them; but, you will excuse me, sir—you was so jolly 'green ' I thought you must be one of the gang." As she was about to pass him he said, looking archly at her, "Oh, you pretty, pretty, la.ss 2" The girl tossed her head, and replied, '‘l am sorry I can. not return the compliment !" " Faix, you could If you had lied as I did," said he, as he walked away from the indignant maid.

Next in order of u3efulnees to a black woollen gown is a navy or periwinkle blue and white foulard, which may advisedly be made with a flounced skirt, and a bodice with yoke of ivory or yellow lace over white satin' or it can be trimmed with rows of inch-wide blue ribbon slightly gathered along the top edge, and the yoke replaced by a vest of mousseline-de-soie.

To don on chilly evenings with one of these foulard gowns a pretty little cape of blue cloth piped with white is a desirable poasession and rot a very costly one. Little coats of coloured cloth, too, are very popular to wear over the smarter class of woollen, or the plainer kind of silk gowns, and they are often elaborately braided or covered with chenille embroidery.

The new plain kilt cut in one length, and with the usual gores, i 3 now only found at the advanced modistes' as a foundation to an elaborate overpart, and the skirt proper is now cut in several tiers or sections. One of the newest skirts has the top and front made and fitted, and the flounce is made and trimmed separately, and then put on over the upper part. If of thin, fragile, or stretch- able material, lining and material should be made together, otherwise the flounce and its lining are separate at its edge and this gives a more fashion- able effect. The b'odice is exceedingly becoming with revere overlaid with motifs of lace, and these are also arranged to simulate a very abbreviated bolero.

For swimming costumes young girls are wearing princesse or combination garments, terminating in very full knickerbockers, with, a broad soft sash or belt loosely fastened round the waist. Bathing toilettes are, however, universally made with a skirt or tunic, and these vary in style, many reach- ing quite to the knee, and others only midway between knees and waist. Some, too, are gored off sharply to the waist, like a fashionable dress, while others are slightly gathered all round, and make the hips appear round and waist small. Leather belts, drawn exceedingly tight, are fool. ishly affected by the young ; but the serge band, mounted on buckram or folded linen, is less in- jurious, and has a more natural effect. Your loving JENNIE.

FIG PIIDDING.—Chop 4oz. of figs into dice- shaped pieces, mince 4oz. of suet; take 4oz. of breadcrumbs, 4oz. golden syrup, and mix all together with two beaten eggs. Put all into a greased mould, cover with greased paper; tie over a clean cloth wrung out of cold water, pull over the corners and pin. Boil for two hours.

Several members of our Royal Family have been en- joying a comparatively secluded life of late,much to the regret of the public, but to their own great delight. Accustomed from infancy to a life of publicety and homage, it seems curious that Royalty should ever suffer from that affliction which so frequently assails less exalted individuals—very shyness. Yet it is a well- known fact that not a few of our Princessee suffer consi- derably from nervousness, and dread intense'y, an appearance in public. Among the Queen's daughters, Princess Henry of Battenbere is urquestionably the most shy and nervous and 'econcerning the Sovereign's grandefaughters, the Duchess of Fife may be said to head the list in this par- ticular way. The Duckees avoids every court function she possibly cen, and leads the very quietest of lives. In appearance Her Royal Highness becomes more and more like Ler mother, the Princess of Wales, and this year she has look very charming and girlish in the ex- quisite white toilettes she invariably affects. To Princess Victoria of Waive a public appearance is always torture, and the Duchess of Connaught is very similarly constituted. To escape from court formalities and to be free to enjoy the quiet cut-door life she loves so well, is to her—bliss. The Duchess from a very early age, has teen a fearless rider,aed she si's eer horse with considerable grace and dignity. The Greek bazaar, in aid of Greek induetries,recently held at Mr. Ruben Sassoon'e beautiful London house,was a greill success. The Princess of Wales looking very sweet and gracious, in a gown of mauve and white foulard, trimmed with cream lace,and a teepee to match with uo-standing orchids on one eide, accompanied her niece, the Duchess of Sparta, who opened the bazaar. stall holders were all women known in the smartest f WS, and the Royal folks, during their tour of the room levinced the greatest interest in all they saw, and made numerous purchaser. During the present month, Lord Leighton's house at Kensington which is being clowly adapted for use 58 a museum has been open to the public on Wednesdays and Saturdays. and has been visited by hundreds who, before, ccly knew the ereat painters famous and beauti- ful house by repute. At present this remains essentially unaltered, on the stairway stands Mr. Brock's bust of the painter, and the fountain sines as of olden the Arab sal. In the tipper rooms, 6tudies reprgeeuting every phase of Lord Leighton's work are placed round the proof prints of his pictures, thus showing how the sub• jet grew in the artist's mind. Mrs. Lynn Linton whose death has just occured, at the age of seventy-five, entered upon her literary career at the age of twenty-three, and she claimed to be one of the first three wemen to write for the Louden daily press. One•among the many "crazes"she had supreme contempt for was—interviewing. She considered the wbole business a fraud and a nuisance. The craze for mi,sionary work too, in unlikely, and unsympathetic counties, she was sternly against, and so far as the craze for cycling is concereed, Mrs. Linton considers the exercises a queer CNN between the treatmill and the tight-rote. But despite this sweeping condemnation of our present favourite form of recreation, cycling still flourishes, and the woman who fails nowadays to possess a bicycle, is indeed, hopelessly behind the times. Both the wife and daughter of M. Alma Tadema are devoted tc cycling,and have lately become members of the Cyclists ' Touring Club,and Miss Olga Netheesole firmly believes' in the benefits of the exercise. Cycling is doing more far OUT NM than most of us recognise, and without doubt it is helping largely to lift us from that slough of (Meese, into which, according to some of:our critics.we women Of the British Isles are Sunk. Summer sates are in full swing, and "Sweeping Re- ductiees "the order of the day. Of source the bloom— as uival—has been rubbed off most of the articles rffered, but this is mere detail to the sale-lover. Per- sonally, I have never found these functions a success— and now make a point of carefully avoiding them. It is possible I know, to occasionally come across a genuine " t.argain," at such times, but taking into consideration the mete and scramble one has to endure to seeure Petrie raid bargain always seems to -ne dear at the price. That the eonatantly recurring " sales "are of great henefit to bopkepppre, there can be not the smallest doubt,but the majority of women wile patronise them could possibly tell another tale—if they would. One of the things to be avoided at sale times, is the eurchase of trimmed millirery. " Reduced " headgear is invariably, unwearable, an item we can scarcely mar- vel at, when we come to consider that the hats teques, and bonnets offered, have been in and out of boxes, en I and off stands and heads. and more or less exposed to , the dust, for a season. Fruit figures extensively in the millinery of the mdment, as do also euinea-fowl feathers which are introduced with any schemes of color. They have a certain silvery valtee, and look especially well with white lie, or yellow tulle toques. For evening wear, wired gauze bows perched right in front of the coiffure, are much en evidence. In black, these transperent little items are usually becoming ; but the tinsel specimens are not desirable additions to one's toilette. Many of our most modish women are patronising the nest coil worn low in the neck, but the higher and more elaborate arrangement is still in force in the fashionable world. One reason for this probably is that the style suits the majority better,and further, it lends itself so well to the adjustment of .aigrettes, jewelled ornaments, tiaras, etc. The markets for the trading in and distribution of precious stenes,have changed since olden times. Tyre, Alexandria, Rome Constantinople, have all had their turn. 'Venice held sway in the middle ages for a time, rid Augsburg was a great centre. Eastern explorations carried the market to Colombo, Goa, and Golconda. In recent times Amsterdam and Antwerp have been prime centres for diamonds especially, but Paris and London now rule. By young girls, semi-precious stones are being much worn, In the form of necklets and bracelets. These stones include the amethyst and the topaz, as well as those curious antique gems, which are known by such strange names as the " zircon." the " peridot," and the "obsidian," and which are of the quainteet and most fascinating colours imaginable. Both the Duchess of Portland and Lady Granby, have a great affection for thee aneient stones, of which they possess some very perfect specimens . Pearls should be exposed to the air as much as pos- sible, and never by any chance damped. A sunhath does them a world of good except in very hot weather. Ooals, the best of which by the way, are obtained from Hungary and Honduras, must be kept from fire and heat, ass high temperatuie renders them liable to split. Torquoisevhould never be wetted—such a proceeding rendering ern liable to change (intone.

THE _EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JULY 22, 1898. (cvright.) A WARD OF THE KING. '•BY KAWARINE S. MACQUOID, Anthorsof'"liiisie Derrick," "The Story of Lois,* "Patty," "Louisa," "At the Red Glove," "Miss Eyon of Eyoncourt," 45cc.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Jeanne Kergrist, a wealthy heiress and an only. child, has become on her father's death ward of the King of France. Jeanne is only thirteen when the -King commands her to marry the Count of Laval, who i• twenty years her senior. The story opens in i- agrden of Jeanne's house, where Jeanne tells her friend and playfellow Rolland of her dislike to the proposed marriage. Rolland, a fine young fellow, dislikes it too. He has been brought up with Jeanne, and, if he were richer, would marry her when she grows up. The Count of Laval comes to the castle accompanied by a handsome young cousin, Gilles de Retz. Jeanne like the Count, but she takes a dislike to De Retz, who flatters and pities her. He and the Count of Laval leave the castle directly after the marriage ceremony. Four years later, Jeanne's mother dies. Rolland has been away fighting in Italy and the Netherlands. Jeanne is alone in the world and her husband falls ill. He sends de Retz to fetch his young wife home to Laval. Jeanne is seventeen and has become beauti- ful. She travels in a litter to Laval, accompanied by her maids and her mother's woman Gillonne, a courageous and clever Bretonne. They reach Laval at the end of fourr days and learn that Jeanne's husband the Count is dead. De Retz is now Count of Laval, and Gillonne suspects his intentions ,towards her mistress. She resolves to seek help and advice from her widowed mistress's friend Rolland, who has now become h Viscount. Jeanne asks the Count of Laval to take her to Amboise to seek pro- tection from her guardian the King. Laval consents.
CHAPTER VII. GILLONNB'g ADYZATITRE.

When she had made all ready for the journez, Gillonne left her mistress and found her way to te, guard-room. Gildas was standing before the. entrance, and she inquired of him where She WOUI find Monsieur de Retz. The man looked at her; then he said signifi- cantly. "You should call folks by their right names, Mistress Tirewomanl You will find his nobleness the Count of Laval in the office of the Seneschal, but lam not certain that he can attend to you; it is a busy morning with us all." Gillonne thanked him, and hurried along a narrow passage--on the previous evening she had learnt where to find the Seneschal. She thought herself lucky to meet the young Count coming towards her. Gillonne was clever as well as shrewd, but, like many another woman, she had carefully thought out her plans only from her own point of view. Therefore, when she had preferred her request to the Count, she was utterly disconcerted to hear that Gildas could not possibly be spared to accompany her. "I have other work for him," the Count said pleasantly, though Gillonne felt sure he was enjoy- ing her disappointment. "You are welcome to have Philippe and Claspard ;I will at once give orders to that effect." " He turned abruptly back to the Seneschal's office. Gillonne stood dumbfounded. She had already noticed Philippe, a poor, deaf, ill-looking fellow; while she had conceived a strong dislike for Gas- pard. During the journey he had seemed to be one of the most trusted followers of De Retz, a lithe, dark-eyed, insolent soldier. She had more than once said to herself he was a likeness of the Evil One. she secretly crossed herself as he passed her by. Gillonne's father and her brothers had all been fighting men, and as a child she had eagerly listened to their tales of stratagem employed in the taking of towns and fortresses. She had made up her mind to reach the Chateau d'Orbec and either there or elsewhere to get speech with its lord. She could have trusted Gildag, but she saw that with a man like Gaspard she must be wary; he must not have an inkling that she was bound for anywhere but for her cousin's house in Mayenne. It was true that she had a cousin in Mayenne, her grandfather had inhabited that part of France; but Gillonne thought it possible that this cousin might have died, it was so long since she had heard of him. In that case, unless she managed warily, she should perhaps be expected to return with her escort, whereas her fixed intention was to proceed to the Chiteau d'Orbee with as little delay as possible. She hdd' learnt that Orbec was on that side of Lisieux nearest to Mayenne. Gillonne had plenty of courage, and she felt excited by the diffi- culties of her expedition as she climbed the wind- ing staircase to her mistress's chamber. , • The sky was grey and lowering when the party started, but all the women were shielded by heavy cloaks, which wrapped them from head to foot ad effectually concealed their Sgures., The Countess wore a black riding-mask, which covered the upper part of her face, and her saddle and horse trap- pings were richly ornamented; otherwise there was nothing to distinguish her from Gillonne and hs. two maids. Just before they reached a road which opened on the left at a short distance from the Castle the soldier Gaspard rode up, followed by deaf Philippe. De Retz—or the Count of Laval, as he was now called—was riding beside the Countess. "This, madame," he said, "is your woman's escort,' _ _

Jeanne stretched out her hand; Gillonne bent down and kissed it; then,' drawing the hood of her cloak round her face, the woman rode away with her two guardians. Gillonne was taking herself to task about her secret fears.

"What can harm me if I free myself from their tiresome company?" she asked. "I am a good horsewoman, I am strong, I have no sense Of fear; I am forty, but I can climb and scramble as if I were a girl." • She remembered as she rode along that the country south of Lisieux was flatter than that she was now traversing, and that it would therefore be less easy to avoid pursuit in the event of her escape from her escort. As a girl she had travelled with Madame Kergrist from Alencon to the ClAteau d'Orbec, and she remembered that they had fol- lowed a straight and monotonous road, which went northward all the way. If she could get to Alencon, she knew that she could find her way to. Orbec. The cousin she was going to seek at Mayenro had been a native of Alencon •, if she failed to fine him at Mayenne, why not seek him out at his birth- place? This being settled, Gillomie began to listen to the talk of her companions, Philippe's deafness made Gaspard quite audible, as he ridiculed hit companion s last assertion. "Morbleu, I tell you they will not go to Arnboise ; they would have their journey for nothing if they did. The King is at Moulins; I heard my lord say as much to the chaplain before we quitted Laval." She saw a dogged look spread over Philippe's face.

• "They must in that case go by Blois; Amboise is out of the road. Till they reach Blois there is not a high-road to Moulins. But why does the King go to see the Constable at Moulins? There is not much love lost between them, if report says true." •

Gaspard sneered. "My good friend, when a man loses his hearing he should be chary of his words. Know, my too wise Philippe, that cothmon report says the Constable has turned traitor; he has sided with the accursed English swine and the German fox against his sworn lord and master, the King of France." Philippe answered in a sullen tone: "I do not believe it I I have served under the Duke of Bourbon • so brave a General cannot hat.; turned traitor( Gfratid Diable Do you mean tr tell me the King has gone to Moulins to put the Constable under arrest? " Gaspard nodded.

"Nom de Dieu! I should like to be there "—his voice sounded fierce—"there will be rare fighting before the King can capture the Constable in his own city of Moulins! Maybe we shall get tidings at Mayenne ; the mistress at the Croix d'Or is a rare wench for gleaning news." To this Philippe answered doggedly: "Women know nothing truly, curse them! They make up tales; they will not own they have naught to toll." After this they rode on in silence. They took no more heed of Gillonne than if she had been a bundle of goods on the horse that bore her. When they slackened their pace to mount another hill, she looked round at Gaspard. "Did I understand you to say the King is not at Amboise? "

He gave her an insolent glance. "Likely enough you did, mistreal ; the news has been common talk ever since we left St. Brieuc. You might have seen a messenger bring tidings to the Count of Laval as we rode away from the town. Poor Philippe here gathers up news when the rest of the world has done with it." Philippe looked uneasy: he hen;-1 his own name,

out he could not make out the rest. He glanced first at Gillonne„ then at Ga;spard. "The Xing will have gone to Moulins to learn the truth," Gillonne said. "He is ever on the side of mercy." Gespard -again looked at her with all the insolence he feltif.i.t,heving beenfiegraded to take charge of en *old viojnan, as he' celled Gillonne. He had taken a fancy to Anne, and he had promised him- self some pastime with the young girl; he laid his disappointment to Gillonne, and he was very surly with her.

"Say you so, mistress? You seem learned in the ways of Sings I It will; be a: long ride to ' Moulins for your lady." Gillonne took the alarm he intended to give her. "Do you mean that my lady will be taken direct to Moulins, instead of to Amboise ? "

She could not entirely hide her dismay, and the soldier laughed loudly. "Cheer up, old girl! Your pretty lady is safe with our Count, I warrant! When he has finished the business he has in hand, belike he will wed her, and take her with him to Laval. You may be sure the King will sanction the marriage." He again laughed brutally. Gillonne would not answer; she was glad that the rapidly-failing light hid her face, for she felt that it must shew her angry feelings. She thought she had been unwise in leaving her mis- tress; her plan might after all fail, for it was possible she might not find Rolland de Ds Touche at the Chateau d'Orbec.

There has been a perfect glut of strawberries this year hit the season for this delicious fruit is always a short I one, and they are quickly gone and forgotten, save as jam. This year they came to an end smoner than usual, for want of moisture, but the spell of fine dry weather which set in with July has greatly inproved tho prospect 1 of the fruit season generally, and from the housekeepers point of view, the tre fruits are the more important. The orchards in some parts of the country appear to be faihres, but despite this, the probability is that there will be a superabundance of pears, apples and plums. I They will he plentiful for a time, and cheap, but cur farmers do out give much attention to growing and storirg fruit, and it is never very long before we have to fall back upon the important foreign supplies. Most people when going into the country at this time of the year for their holidays, take an interest in the state of the crops and harvest prospects generally, and consider- ing all the vicissitudes which beset the farming indus- try it is gratifying to hear that it promises to be a good agricultural year. Those fortunate peeple who can obtain cherries in almost unlimited quantities are wise if they bottle a gcod supply, bottled fruit being an eminently usefhl way of storing up all store fruit. Here is a reliable recipe Pill widernouthed bottles with sound ripe cherries from which remove the stalks without breaking the fruit. Put two tablespoonfuls of castor sugar into each bottle, cork them tightly, put the bottles standing up right, hit° a pan of cold water, let the water come slowly to boiling point, sod boil five minutes. Then removing the pan to one side, leave the bottles standing in the water until they have become quite cold,wipe the bottles dry, tie paper over the tops, and pack away in a dry store cupboard.

div.head: CHAPTER VIII.
div.p: CHAPTER VIII.

•T THE CROIX D It had become quite dark by the time the reached Mayenne; that is to say, it was dark in the narrow, twisting street that led from the town gate. Gillonne felt that she'had better wait till' morning before she went in search of her cousin.. But at the Croix d'Or there was far more light; for the dirty-looking hostel stood on a bit of waste beside the town, and had no houses near it. A stout, fair-haired woman, with handsome, shameless blue eyes, came out to receive them—this was the hostess—and she flung both arms round Gaspard when he dismounted. "-Welcome, welcome, my soldier!" she cried. "You are truly a sight to heal sore eyes!" He kissed her heartily, and inquired for the patron. "Eh—the imbecile! He is at Javron—rns9 503` go with him! He has to take a waggon load of slates to Lisieux, for the roof of the Maison Valois." She caught sight of Gillonne's cloaked figure—" Holy Virgin t what have we here?" "Foul! she's only someone I have to escort home to her friends here in Mayenne." , The woman came forward she held up the candle she carried, till the light fall full on Gillonne's pale, plain face; then she turned away with a laugh. "Is that all ? No younger than that. You good-for-nothing, I thought I had caught you at your tricks again!" Then to Gillonne: "Welcome, madame." She curtseyed. "Will yo ti like to come and -see your chamber?" Gillonne was tired by her long ride, and she gladly followed the woman into the house and up some dirty stairs. The room above was a miserable garret, open to the rafters; here and there she saw wide cracks between the planks of the dirty floor. The bed, however, looked fairly clean. Gillonne seated herself on a rough bench, and the hostess set down the light she carried on a table in the window.
"I will fetch madame when supper is served, or else I will send Henriot."

"Thank you, Madame, but I am over-tired; s crust of bread and a cup of wine will be enough. I can eat here if you will send it to me." She shrank from the touch of the shapely hands busy in unfastening her cloak. The woman seemed to feel this; he looked fixedly at Gillonne's dark-browed, ascetic face, reddened, and said with a scoff: "Bread and wine, ask you, mother? Mon .Dieu! we can better that at the Croix d'Or! We keep no fast-days here, good dame!" Gaspard's voice came loudly up the stairs. "There, there, be patient; I come—l come!" _
_ "Louise, Louise where have you hidden your- self? I want wine—wine--the best you can find in the cellar! I'll wager the patron has left you the lug ?", _ _ _

Gillonne was glad to be left alone. She found it difficult to shut her ears to the unsavoury talk that came up from the room below. She went to the window and looked out; there was not much light, but she saw below her a yard round which the house seemed to be built. Sounds:from ,an open door in the opposite building shewed her that it was the stable, but while she looked an appetising fume from below told that supper was in progress, and somewhat of a lull came in the laughing dialogue between Gaspard and his hostess: .• The woman came presently upstairs; and entered - without knocking. She held in one hand a trencher full of savoury stew, and in the other a cup of wine ; she brought also a knife and a long brown loaf.,
"Will this serve your turn, mistress ? " she asked.

"Thank you; it is excellent. Good-nigkit to you," she said. "I am weary aud shall be glad to sleep when I have supped. Good-night, and thank you."Gillonne tasted the food, and found it better than she had expected; the wine was rough, but it was drinkable, and she felt greatly refreshed by the time her supper was over. Then she sat and planned her future proceedings. It has been said that she was observing and courageous; she was also extremely sagacious; and she had the habit of noting and pieceing together small facts, the habit so remarkable in experienced upper servants, especially in French servants. She sat thinking out the events of the day, and the retrospect did not give her trust in Gaspard. He must have seen that she was high in favour with her mistress; how, then, had he ventured to speak to her so insolently? Seemingly, he did not fear that she might complain of his conduct on her return. A. cold chill seized on Gillonne ;it is true that the chamber felt both cold and damp, but not enough to make her shiver violently, while her teeth chattered. It came to her as a certainty that De Retz, or Laval, suspected her distrust of him; if he meant to wed her lady, as Gaspard said, he probably wished to be rid of her trusted waiting-woman. While she sat thinking, Gillonne felt colder and colder. She had meant to rise before the house was astir, and try to find her kinsman. If she could not find him, she had fancied, when she learnt the change of route, that it would be wiser to give up her plan, and travel back with the two soldiers to her mistress— for Gaspard had let her see how impatient he was to rejoin his company. The noise of a dispute below disturbed her meditation; the hostess was seemingly excusing herself. Then came Gaspard's hearty laugh. "Off with you, saucy mistress! Bring more wine—and, look you, clear your house as soon as may be; my comrade here is sleepy, and I want a word with him before he turns in. Get you gone, Louise, I say!" The door was slammed to; then mine a pause of silence.

Gillonne heard a stealthy movement below; the door was sottly opened and closed. Her heart beat quickly as she glanced at her own door; she had put a bar across it when her hostess left her. She was, however, soon reassured; Gaspard's voice below shewed her that he had merely looked out to be safe from listeners. •

—"Philippe!" The sound came up to her some- what muffled; she thought his lips n'inst be close to his companion's ear. "Wake up and listen! Monsieur le Comte told me he did not care to see that old woman again. Do you understand ? " "Yes," came sleepily from Philippe. "Well, after what she learnt this afternoon, the old woman will try to get back as soon as she can to her mistress. We can make sure of her horse, but she is a woman with nimble wits. Morbleu I have noticed that the older a woman grows, the sharper grow her wits; it is the compensation for the loss of all excuse for her existence." His next words came in so muffled a lone, that Gillonne laid down noiselessly to the floor, and placed herb ear close to one of the broad cracks. "Look you, Philippe, if this charge of ours ever catches sight of her mistress again, we shall both smart for it. What say you, bully? What shall we do ? "

Philippe muttered so indistinctly, that she could not hear his answer. She pressed her hands together; they were clammy with fear. Gaspard laughed out. "That is to the point my friend; I knew you would not stick at trifles ! "
_ Philippe's monotonous voice again broke the silence. This time she heard what he said.

"There is only one way, Gaspard, and you know it. Mark you, there is more in it; there is profit i'or both of us. The old dame carries a purse at her girdle, I saw it, and I warrant 'tis well 4inedl "
liaspard seemed to break into his comrade's orsmda.

"Enough; we have got to leave a silent toque Jehind us, and then we ride for the Count. X" must sleep here- till morning. I have to see Louise. In the morning she shall bid the old woman seek for her cousin. Listen: you and I will follow her; there is more than one quiet corner in Mayen'e were we can settle our little matter without fear of witnesses." - ,

• Heavy steps crossed the room below; a door wae opened and closed, but the steps did, not corae upstairs—they died away into stillness The shivering woman lying prone on the floor above, fancied they did not leave the house. She softly rose and blew out her candle. She felt stupefied with terror; but as she moved softly fp the window hope and courage came back. Sha stared down into the darkness.; there was not a light to be seen in any of the windows. "I have the night before me," she thought; "if I can only get out of the house, I may be mileo away before morning." A sound in the room made her start; she held her breath and listened. A scuttling across the floor reassured her. Presently a prolonged snore from the room below told her that the deaf man was asleep. Gillonne sat perfectly still for more than art hour; the heavy snoring came through the floor at intervals. At last she thought the time had come, and she gently unbarred her door and opened it. The same discordant sounds came from other chambers, else all was still.

The Breton woman groped till she found the cloak she had laid aside; she put it on, and open- ing the front of her woollen robe, she drew forth a sheathed dagger; she stuck this into the girdle that secured her purse to her waist, wondering how Philippe had seen it; she had thought it Was concealed by the folds of her cloak. Gathering this closely round her, she went out on to the rickety staircase, careful of every footstep, for, as she came up, she had noted the decayed condition of the stairs.

It was not easy to find her way in the darkness, but her shrewd wit helped her, and she felt con- fident there would be no bars or bolts between the house and the stables. She had reached the passage at the foot of the staircase, and was moving softly along it, her heart beating loudly; she suddenly stopped. A strange sound came from the right side of the passage. Sick with terror, Gillonne leant against the wall, clutching at her dagger. A momenee listening told her the sound was a series of drunken hiccoughs from some slumberer in a chamber beside the passage. She again went stealthily on till she reached the end of the passage. As she had expected, the door was unbarred; it opened easily. She closed it behind her, and the keen air. told her she was in the courtyard. A fresh terror seized Gillonne at the sight of a light in the stab opposite; only a faint glimmer through the gratink but if anyone were sleeping in the stable, she felb that she was lost. She waited till her eyes became accustomed to the darkness ; there were stare shirting brilliantly overhead, and presently the made out the stable door on one side of the grating. She cautiously opened the door and looked /0; no sleeper was to be seen. She blessed the dile, lantern hanging ,from the wall, its light enable her to find,-her own horse without delay. Os saddle and bridle hung beside him. The intelligent creature recognised her voice, Oa licked her hand. Gillonne loved horses, and ell felt at home in a stable. She quickly bridled ac; saddled the horse, and then led him quietly e 5,.." till they had passed under the arched entrance "' the courtyard. She led him on a few paces past the Croix wor; climbed into her saddle, and rode. away. She bee, noted her hostess's words about a waggon load 13,' slates which her husband was next morning to tO,e from iavron to Lisieux. In old days she had ma° the journey with her mother from Mayenne tO Alencon, and she rememhered that Javron lay be; tween the two places, considerably nearer Mayecsj than it was to Alencon. Instead of losing time e, 1,. seeking her cousin, she resolved to take the road w, Jayron, and to get there before the waggon starter" She did not fear pursuit; Gaspard, she felt would lose some time in seeking her at her cousic house. As soon as she was clear of the inn, she lookecl round her. She was 'still on the strip of waste lel and as she looked right and left in the starlightje she recognised the five pointed caps of the cO., towers, and two heavy masses of building she knew were the ancient Churches cif Mte/71e She was trying to find out the directiolq:.;age river; she remembered that once across the "'" over the Mayenne, the road on her left would ti:be her direct to Javron ; but she was Pueele'r by 'be ease with which.she had reached the outside of t e town, for the Cnstle and the churches seemed sowle_ distance off. Last night they had entered the to from-the west, and had passed through gear",,, gateway. A sudden flash of memory reminded tu.f anxious woman that the ruined wall at this part (1, the town had not been rebuilt when the °thee fortifications were repaired because the cl°st proximity of the river made it secure; she ran therefore be near the bridge, and she would fin° 1 guarded. She rode on some way further. Yes, there ltio the river before her, gleaming in the starlight; bridge must be round the bend which the strei' made to the left. mho She checked her horse, and sat thinking. summer had been dry, and she could see that Mayenne at this point was not nearly so broad ; stream as it had been at Laval. Gillonne resolre: to try and cross it on horseback'; she gathered 140 her cloak and skirts, and rode for about a leag% along the waste which ended in a high bank abev, the river; then slae saw that the ground took,; gentle slope downwards, till it reached the water,i, edge. Gillonne reined in her horse, and devos" crossed herself. "I commit myself to God, to His Blessei Mother, and to holy St. Catharine." She bee forward, and patted her horse's neck. "Courage' my friend, and take me safely over." The horse seemed to know that she had abes.; doned herself to his guidance. He placed :1/11, feet cautiously as he crossed the stream, in wit'cy countless stars were reflected. The scorching be; of the previous month had shrunk the Mayences, tributaries to mere rivulets, and the river was o.°o a 'shallow stream, choked in some places WI pebbles. Gillonne could hardly believe in her safety 'eV; she reached the opposite bank. The horse ehoere himself, and gave a low whinny, as if he weto satisfied. She had yet to find the road Alencon • she had called to mind there was anotrat road leading to the south on this side of it. ." she could not mistake; the Alencon road wee_a highway, rough, but too much used to be cumbei—pe with stones, as the narrow road might be;. it 11,A also free from the quagmires which she remetaben— used to exist on this side of Mayenne. starlight* So she quickly rode on in the glittering

--- Town councils and all local bodies throughout country cannot lay to heart too closely the decision of a Committee of the House of Commons, Who have refused the vestry of Marylebone, a Lon- don parish, permission to instal electric light Within its own area, because it had already con- Ilentedi to the werk being undertaken by a private pany. This is not like the decision of a court, or it does not bind another committee In another. liession any more than it binds another Parlia- Enent. It is a danger with which town councils 'aye to reckon whenever they happen to he in a L.Asition like that of the vestry of Marylebone. 'theY must first buy out the company they have licensed or sanctioned before they can remove the tight to provide a municipal installation. It is P°lble that the House might not confirm the coda_ Mittee's finding, and if local bodies were sufficiently Urban members might be alarmed for their seats snd vote accordingly ;", but it would be more to the Point if local bodies would definitely make up their mind whether they will keep the Dower in "leir own hands or make it over to a company,

With this end in view rheurnatisua " settled "in poor Lear's hips and legs. Slowly but surely it proceeded to destroy his power to walk. The young legs, once so supple and elastic, became weaker and weaker. But the collapse was not immediate ; it seldom is. It took about sixteen monthe to bring it to pass. -During this time, especially the latter portion of it, he realised the blessing of having a good wife ; and if any man has one, Lear has ; the writer has seen her, and knowc It was this faithful and loving woman who literally supported ber husband as his pain increased and s strength declined. It was on her shoulder that he leaned in his walks out of doors, and in his efforts to earn much-needed shillings. So between the two of them they managed—with the help given them by people who pitied tnem—to keep a loaf on the table and the wolf from the door. But this must not be over- eatimated by the reader; they did.not starve but they often went hungry.

Meanwhile, however, how about trying to get relief from the disease ? He did try,of course—tried in every direction that was open to him. Neighbours gave him of their medicines ; liniments, embrocations, ointments, and salves, to rub on the inflamed joints and the sore muscles ; and advised many sorts of treatment they had heard or read of. Slight and transient relief followed the use of some of these things without doubt, but the progress of the ailment was not checked, It was like a great army that marches on in spite of skirmishing on its flanks.

Through the influence of the Rev. Mr. Wilson, minis- ter of the Woolwich Tahernacle,where Leah and his wife both attend,the poor fellow was provided with letters to the Military and also the Seamen's Hospital at Wool- wich,and was treated at both these excellent institu- tions ; unhappily without any material benefit. He afterwards attended at the London Hospital with the same result. _

" The doctors at all the hospitals," be says, "and also the doctors in private practice who prescribed for me, were as Wad as though I had been a rich man, but bald out no hope of my ever getting well. On this the terri- ble truth struck my mind as it had not done before ; I was doomed to be a cripple for life,and it was no use to fight against my fate. 6 I must tell you," added Leah, that I had the rheu- matism bad in my left arm and to some extent in my right. So, all I should have left to work with would be, as you may say, about half of one arm. " It was on March 2nd, 1897, that I gave up and took t; the crutchee. Thank God, I am dooe with them now. I gave them to lir. Robert J. Todd, of 2, Collingwood- street, Woolwich, S.E., for the use of lais brother-in-law, wha is a cripple, but not on account of rheumatism." It will be surmised by the intelligent reader that dur- ing his tedious illness—so full of pain, so intesified by poverty, so crowned at last by despair—that Matthew Lear was laid helpless on his bed,in the poor little room I have told you of,tinses beyond counting. The neigh- boure' children shouted at play in the street not a yard rem his laced, the women of the vicinity stood about and gossipPed, and mornings came and also the nights, and now and thee a funeral passed drearily by, Sundays dawned with chiming bells, and holidays with the noise of people making merry ; still Matthew lay on his bed; rising once and again (helped b n y his patient wife)— rlciasets y' with sighs and groans and crawling back h and sighs.This.sometitries, for weeks in sec- rwi with cession. His heart troubled him too, heating feebly as if it had half a mind to stop altogether. If it had stoprr6d nobody would have wondered, for often did the neigh- bours fancy they saw grim death,in the form of a gent. in black, writing in a little book,

A cat means to eat her mouse, bat she plays with it first. The velvet paw, the h armless cuffs and taps— then ihe sharp tohite teeth. Alas !we know. The coa- ti mptivo is always " a bit better " till he dies, and the woman over whose eves cataract is weaving its filnay c urtains sees a trifle more clearly than yesterday, until she tits alone ia a dark world. God help us ! Row awful are the possibilities of eVn the simplest lives. Early in the autu na of 1897 L acr lett his bed and he- can selling shoe laces, as we h eve snen him. But not steadily: From time to time he broke dowo, as he d d later the sante season, being shut up at home, suffering and lamenting, as bef ore, many days. Ah, there was mu ch to bear, little to hope for, less to get. What could a peer emaciated cripple do ? He could let himself degrees—like a man descending "The profits on all the shoe laces I could sell," said all be he could do. about never have made the pet coam butvte admovawo tpnt ah ion; wtt bswe I tar the money that was given me by charitable people in the etreet." I Then came the incident, already recorded, of the I stranger who gave him the shilling wherewith to buy a I medicine the name of whieh was written on a piece of I paper. That medicine proved to be Mother Seigel's Syrup, and he got his first bottle (with all that followed) men Messrs. Goldthorpe and Cook, 37, Hare Street, Woolwich. He used it and it relieved his rheumatism, and e specially abated the dyspepsia, from which he had suffered !madly before the rheumatism came upon bins, and afterwards continuously with it. Ile took this svVite, four months- -eliet remedy, and no ether, thereafter unntilheide store twelve.of C Thee p t ti m bottles—all e vve vt,d nearly,dl y pee or r ender the circumstances, a wonderful result. Then he gave away 'his crutches, and has had no need of them since. I The poison in this man's blood—the result ot chronic dyspepsia and the cause of rheumatism—was expelled by Mother Seigel's Syrup, and the digestion was nude vigorous and natural. With the renewing power of digested food came strength, and the cripple, whose ease was alleged to be incurable, note walks as other men. Now, from reading the other story you may be im- pressed with the idea that Mother Seigel's Syrup per- formed something in the nature of a miracle. something wonderf tat, mysterious and hard to understand. But really it did nothing of the kind : it cured a simple disease—namely, indigestion or dyspepsia ; and that being the true cause of rheumatism (and most of our common ailments), Matthew Lear recovered, as one always does, when the cause of his disease is removed. All Who .euffered from any trouble of the stomach or ilver may be cured by Mother Seigel's Syrup. no not wait for the worst and more dangerous results to follow, but stop the misehief at once by taking the medicine when the first symptoms appear. Mother Selgel's Syrup should be in every, home for daily use when needed. Oise more triurnp Li, then, for the true theory of disease, one more victory (added to the theueands) for that standard and successful remedy, Mother Seigel's syrup! Matthew Lear and his wife humbly and devoutly thank God for it; and so, the writer is sure, will the stranger who gave Matthew the good advice and the good shilling that day in the Plumetead Road, should this simple but true story ever meet his eye. Ie and down the long street echoed this cry as Matthew Lear, the man whs uttered it, rneved slowly and painfully on his way ; for he was a cripple. A pair of stout crutches bore the weight of his body, and at every step he helped himself with his right leg, never with the left. Over his shoulder hung a bunch of shoe laces which he was offering for sale to a public that seemed none too eager to buy. Owing, perhaps, to one or more of the various reasons which affect other lines Sr business there appeared to be a small demand for shoe laces that day. Singly or in groups people hurried by without deigning more than a glance at the seller of this simple merchandise, who continual t) beseech attention with the plainzive refrain, " Long Issoliair laces, shoe laces."

The time was the middle of December, the weather cold,dreary and cheerless. I bitter wind was blowing. It made men quicken their pace, and took liberties with the dresses of the ladies who were out shopping for Christi:n*sm near at baud. But only now and then one of these women with well-filled purses were Inclined to invest a penny in shoe laces ; and the man on the ierutchere thumped heavily along the pavement watching ntently for a chance purchaser and droning Ws mono- therms announcement. All day he had gone up and down the Plunsstead-road in the old borough of Wool- wich, and now the early winter night was drawing in. There was still plenty of movement and stir, but it I threw no crumb of comfort in his direction. The publin housee were doing a brisk trade and so were the butcher's stalle. People drank and made ready to eat, and nobody cared whether he might be hungry and thirsty, or not. And he was both ; and tired into the bargain ;so tired that, having sold a pair of laces to a ittle girl who pitied him, he sank down into a sitting posture upon the pavement and placed his crutches to. tether by his side. People passed to and fro and saw him there, hut took little or no heed. Two (a poor woman and a boy) each gave him a halfpenny but wanted no laces. The wind blew keener and colder, and penetrated his insufficient clothing until his very bones felt the ehill of it. Besides he was faint from want of food, having eaten nothing skin morning, and not much then. A few snewkakes were falling now, with a threat of worse weather. Re ached all over with his exertions. Re would go home, yes, home. But what sort of a home was he going ? Was there a firs in it, and supper? No.; likely. now much money had he? Ile took it out and counted it with cold fingers. 'Ninepence, all in o loner, and not more than threepence really his— as profit on sales- A bad, unlucky day ; a kind of day that drives such as he to the almshouse, or into the river. " My missus will not ntalce the pot acorn to-night," he muttered as he slid the coins back inte his pocket, " We shall both yo to bed hungry, as we have often done before. Bat rwilbyo home." Sten:ling to his foot he balaneod bin-pelf on his crutches and looked around—For what? .Isl:teing. What was there to look for enve starvation and death ? Christmastide aim est, too. And tticy soid this was a Cnristian ace cod country !

Is the seller of laci slood there think ing—no, not thinking, only feeling-1 MIR criss 4. the street and same straight up to him, then said, .4' My lad, what has made You a oriPPle? An injury ?" " No, riteumatisin." " D 3 vaa try to care it ? D) you .tAke remedies for it ?"

" You see my way of genial.; a t how should I buy remedies."-? " I know," said the man, "of a medicine that lam sure win help you. I have known it to cure others as bad as you seem to be; I thMk vL do you good. The price is one and three ha'peoce a bottie. If I give you a shilling wilt you add tie rest and get the rn idicine to- night ? I am. 4 vvirkiu.-.-rian rnyeslf,aid u. no moneY to throw away. Will you promisef" "Yes, and thank you kindly."

11 "Da ;o, and tills day may -prova your ivalciost day after all. mere on this bit of paper is tin nmsn of the medicine. All the cheinists sell it. Huy it,anl go home. No, I won't tell you my name; you will probably never see ins again." Passing a shilling iota the lace-seller's hand, the strange mtn departed as ahruply as he came.

"God bless you, anyway," said the poar fallow, as he started off to keep his word. "Though my mate at home ntay not bo able to make the pat steam ta-aight, if this medicine doei for rne what that man says it will, there'd a chance for warmer fires and better feed in days to come."

So saying, he went to a near-by chemist's shop and bought the medicine ; then, swinging his tired body slowly between his sticks, he measured the road to his home. It was only one room, and small at that. There was a bed, a table, two or three chairs, half-a-dozen cheap pictures on the walls, a glass C 333 protecting some flowers wrought of wool, and a few things needful for limited housekeeping. One window admitted light and gave a view (wholly depressing) of the squalid street. The rent was two-and-sixpence a Week, which must be paid whether there was anything to eat or not. And for the last three years of Matthew Lear's life, rent, meat, and bread had come hard—everything had come hard. For he had been ill. Pain had laid its heavy hand on him and pressed him down and weakness had kept him down. It was that which compelled him to give up his work in the Woolwich Arsenal and transformed a bright, brisk young fellow into what we had seen him.

The complaint thut took the manhood out of him dis- ables more people than accident or war. It is an enemy that assaults you, and sometimes lays you low before you suspect its approach. It twists the symmetrical human body into abhorrent shapes ; it robs the flexible Ibands of their cunning and makes them like blocks of wood; it stiffens the strong muscles and shrivels the I warm flesh until it resembles meat; dried and wasted under a desert sun. It inflames the joints until they throb with congested blood,and makes the nerves scream and jump with agony. This is not all. Long continued, it attacks the heart, and sometimes kills as a knife does when the assassin's isand drives the shining steel to the centre of life.

Rheumatism is known to be caused by a poison in the circulation. What is it ? How is it produced ? Im- portant questions. Matthew Lnat's first sense of this malady came to him in November, 1894 ; a damp, cold month in this climate, as everybody knows—the sort of weather that brings out old ailments and digs up ancient pains and twinges that you thought were buried for good and all.

England in full of rheumatic people ; not perhaps becasse the seeds of it are more plentiful here than else- where, but because we have, during an average year. more of the kind of weather that makes the seeds grow than they have in warmer and drier countries. AT] explanation goes with this. Please wait for it a few minutes.

Then, again, rheumatism, like running water, follows the lines at least resistance ; it picks out a man's Weak spots. It says : "I'll drive long screws into that chap's back so he can't be an engine stoker or a porter any longer ; I'll wring that fellow's wrists so that he can't play the fiddle any more : stick hot needles into that athlete' e; right arm and make him stop boxing or throw- ing hammers ; I'll take that wealthy snit well-fed sub- ject of Her Majesty, and so swell his feet and ankles, and so prod the tendons of his heels, that he will lie back in his easy chair and groan. This last man will call his disease gout, and his doctor (a two-guinea-a- visit dootn) will call it gout ; but gout is my scvn twin brother, and it makes no odds." Thus, gsay, rheumatism soliloquises ; but he speaks

SO softly nobody hears his threats. In friend Lear's case the disease entered upon a cam- paign chiety against his locomotory function ; it set out to make a (ripple of him, to give him over to the tender mercies of adverse fortune, to add the weight of onst more mars to the big load carried by Chsrity,

GUARANTEE.
PRESENTATION OF A SILVER CRADLE TO THE MAYOR AND MAYORESS.

Some considerable time has elapsed since a similar function to that which occurred at the Town Hall on Thursday July 14th took place in the municipal life of the Borough. The event was the presentation of a silver cradle to the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Wright) in com- memoration of the birth of their son Denis, daring the Mayoralty. This is the third time in the history of the Borough that a Mayor and Mayoress have been the recipients of a similar trophy from the members of the Riven Council. A sub-committee of the General Purposes Committee was appointed to select the silver cradle and they decided to accept the design of Messrs. William Woods and Son (Alfred Woods) 14, Sankey-street. The cradle which is of solid silver, weighing 80 ounces, is of very elegant design in the Renaissance style. The centre part forms a cradle lined with gold, suitable for a display of fruit or ibwers. There are also four arms or branches springing from the centre piece, sup- porting elegantly chased and saw-pierced dishes for fruit. The upper part of the centre piece is mounted on a very richly chased base supported by four scroll feet, the whole standing upon a Royal blue velvet plinth. The cradle is very handsomely em- bossed and chased with ornamental work with acanthus leaves, and a wrealth of primrose , flowers and leaves, typical of the spring or dawn of life. It bears the Borough Arms emblazoned in enamel in proper heraldic colours, and also the monogram of the recipients' son "D.R.W." The inscription reads as follows :—" Presented by the members of the Town Council:of Warrington to the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Wright) on the occasion of the birth of tneir son Danis, 14th November, 1897." It was originally intended that Thursday's ceremony should take place in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, but as the weather continued fine and warm it was decided to make the presentation on the lawn in Bank Park. Accordingly the party adjourned there,and were photographed by Mr. Thomas Birtles of Sankey-et. Amongst those present were the Mayor and Mayoress and the young son, Aldermen Harrison Sutton, Fran- comb, Blackhurst, Hutchinson, Fairclough, Roberts, Councillors Heaton, Cannel!, Smethuret, Wilkinson, Bennett, Shillcock, Wood, John Evans, Lee, Rogers, !Furness, Edison, Jolley, Barton, Grace, Peacock, F. R. Roberts, John Roberts, James Evans, Rev. Canon Willis (chaplain), Mr J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk), Mr Luke Talbot (chief constable), Mr J Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Mr T Lengdin (borough surveyor), Mr J Sutcliffe (assistant surveyor), Mr H W Langdin, Mr Charles Madeloy (librarian), Mr T Birtles, Mr J E Birtles, Mr Arthur Browne, Mr Whittaker (Manchester),Mr. Brookes (Man- chester), Mr Eugene Sandow, and Mr F G Taylor. Ths duty of making the presentation devolved upon Alderman HAMMON "the father of the Council," who addressed the gathering from his tricycle. He said he had a little duty to perform. He thought the Mayor and Mayoress were entitled to their warmest congratu- lations. (Hear, hear.) That was a day which must give the Mayor and Mayoress very great pleasure and must undoubtedly impress them with the fact that they were surrounded by warm-hearted friends who desired to see them happy, comfortable, and enjoying all the honours which the honourable position they occupied conferred upon them. (Rear, hear.) The duty which devolved upon him (Alderman Harrison) was to present the Mayor and Mayoress in the name of the Town Coun- cil and several friends with that splendid memento of their goodwill and kindness of heart and appreciation of their services. (Applause.) It was a memento of the little gentleman, the announcement of tirhose birth was made in their grand old Parish Church at the time the Mayor and Corporation were attending divine service there. He remembered that his Worship the Mayor was in a state of great exhilaration at the time. (Laughter.) Without further preface be *mild ask the Mayor's and Mayoress's acceptance of the silver cradle,and he hoped they might live long to treasure it as a memento of a very happy period in their municipal experience. He would ask Mr. Stanley Wilson to form- ally hand the present to the Mayoress in his stead, and expressed the wish that the little trophy of the excellent character which the Mayor and Mayoress had earned would be preserved until the end of the chapter. If would not at all surprise him if the Town Council next November showed some reluctance at parting with such a good-looking Mayor and Mayoress. (Laughter.) Re hoped he might have the pleasure of congratulating them again on occupying such a position. (Applause.) Mr. STANLEY WILSON then handed the cradle to the Mayoress. Alderman FAIRCLCMOTS said he endorsed what had just been said by Alderman Harrison. On behalf of the sub- scribers he wished the Mayor and Mayoress long life and proepeeity. He hoped their son might grow up and be a comfort to them all through their days. He was per- fectly certain that they would be pleased if he became Mayor, and they hoped he would fulfil the office as well and as ably as his father. (Applause). Alderman Surrem said there was one observation he would like to make, and no doubt the Mayor and Mayoress would appreciate it, and that was that every member of the Corporation and every principal official had subscribed towards the present. That was the third time a similar ceremony bad been performed On the occasion of so interesting and impertent an event. But he thought they would all agree with him that that was the most important of the three inasmuch as the young worshipful made his appearance in the Diamond Jubilee of Her ;Majesty and in the Jubilee of tire incorporation ef the Borough. (Hear, beer.) Flo hoped both the Mayor and Mayoress would have long to use that handsome present for many years to come, end not only use it but to enjoy looking at it, and that afterwards it might be whom the handed down to the"wyoonulndgtawkoarstlhdeptfluiglia position " n might probably expect fat h whene r hhoandodp oe dn haen d might come o mwei n theth eMapryi zoer ohf itsVfaartrhi en rg tho and. won on this occasion. (Laughter and applause.) The MAYOR, in acknowledging the gift on behalf of the Mayoress and himself, said he had rc.ceived much kindness from the members ofthe Citorwpoouraidtionbesinirapocehse. entered it 16 or 17 years ago, that sibln for him to forget It. He was gled they had recog. nised an old custom of the Corporation that the Mayor- alty should be recognised when a baby was born. He re-echoed the sentiments which had been expressed that the child might grow up and become a Letter man than hie father, and a ueeful citizen to the dear old tewn of Warrington. During his Mayoralty he had received the utmost courtesy and kindness from every member of the Corporation, and the officials of the Corporation—the Town Clerk especially. H 3 thanked most heartily on behalf of his wife and himself, the friends who had sub- s ;ribed to the present. (Applause). The interesting ceremony tnen terminated. Light re- freshments were afterwards partaken of in the entrance hall.

HEAVY DA.AELGES.

One of the most serious fires which has occurred in Warrington for some time past was that which was discovered early on Sunday morning to have broken out on the premises of Messrs. Richmond end Co., Limited, the well-known firm of gas ap- paratus manufacturers, at their principal works in Academy-street. A boy named Whitney who lives in Academy-street appears to have been the first to discover the fire. A few minutes after five o'clock whilst in bed he saw the reflection of a strong light in his bedroom, and on going to the window which is at the back of the house, he saw games issuing front a portion of Messrs. Richmond's premises. With commendable promptness he went downstairs and without even putting his boots on, he mounted his bicycle and rode with all baste to the Fire Engine Station, where be gave the alarm. The fire bell was rung, and a full complement of firemen in charge of Superinten lent Turner turned out with the fire engine "Captain," hose cart, ladders and fire escapes. In the meantime Inspector Taylor and P.C. Taylor arrived at the scene of the fire, and with several voluntary workers and Mr. Wagstaffe, the store keeper,who was in possession of the keys, they entered the office and commenced re- moving the books and papers. The firemen on arrival found that the fine showroom and warehouse, with the packing room behind situated on the north aide of the street were well alight.and flames were then shooting through the roof. Four jets were quickly got to work, an abundant supply of water being ob- tained from the street hydrants. In and about the centre showroom the fire was raging fiercely, and as there was no possibility of the firemen being able to extinguish the flames there, they directed their principal endeavours towards preventing the spread of he fire to the adjoining workshops,offices and store-rooms and other property in the vicinity, including the Salvation Army Barracks. Their efforts in this respect were entirely successful, and the firemen are to be congratulated upon confining the fire to the premises in which it was discovered. Mr. Ransoms, the manager, and Mr.Hughes,the cashier, were early on the scene, and rendered valuable assistance. The office was in great danger of catching ire, but by the timely intervention of the firemen the progress of the fire was checked, and the offices escaped with but slight injury. Mr. Hughes superintended the work of the removal of the books and documents. The fire originated in a show room, which is in the centre of the buildings, but how it was caused everyone is at a loss to know. The central buildings, which were four storeys high, were completely gutted, aid there now only remains the bare walls and a few charred beams of the fine block of buildings which were erected fif- teen months ago. The show rooms which occupied the second floor were handsomely furnished and fitted up, and at the time of the conflagration they contained specimens of the best work produced by the firm. The warehouses were also filled with cooking ranges of all sizes, gas fires, and apparatus of a similar character. Between six and seven o'clock the fire was at its height, sad the roof and floors cellapsed with a loud crash, the contents of the rooms being completely wrecked. The firemen were seriously impeded in their work by the fumes from the electro-plating and lacquering rooms, caused by the burning chemicals. They were how- ' ever,able to prevent he complete destruction of the rooms, and a large number of stoves were saved in the fitting shop. The men worked pluckily the whole of the time. Some of them were injured during the morning, but after being attended to re- turned to their posts. The fire blazed fiercely and spread rapidly on account of the pitchpine beams with which the premises were supported. Taking this into consideration it is remarkable that the extent of the damage was not greater. Several of the directors paid a visit to the ruins on Sunday. The last person to leave the premises on Saturday was Hr. Wagstaffe, the storekeeper, who made a thorough examination before leaving at five o'clock, but at that time he saw nothing unusual. It is usual for some of the men to be working on Saturday afternoon, but on Saturday all the men left shortly after two o'clock. and in the ordinary course of events Mr. Wagstaffe, after visiting the place at five,would not have gone there again until nine o'clock on Sunday morning, to let some of the workmen in. At four o'clock on Sunday morning Councillor Dr. Cannell, who lives opposite to the works, happened to be up and at the front door of his house, but he observed nothing of an untoward nature. Police-Sergeant Dean passed along the street shortly before five o'clock,and his suspicions were not aroused but within a few minutes afterwards the central buildings were ablaze. The firemen remained at the works during the whole of Sunday, prepared for any fresh outbreak, and rendering what assistance they could in clear- ing the buildings. They returned to the fire station at seven o'clock in the evening, bat an hour and a half later they were re-called, in consequence of an outbreak of fire among the debris in the packing room. This had been smouldering throughout the day. They subdued the flames, and left a couple of men who remained on the premises until half-past six, on Monday morning. About nine o'clock a telephone message was received at the station of a further outbreak, and the firemen again turned out and stayed at the works until dinner-time, but nothing of a serious nature happened. It is fortunate that the fire was confined within the limits it was or a large number of men would have been thrown out of employment. The Com- pany were able to accommodate the workmen whose workshop had to be closed in consequence of the fiemen other parts of the works, and on Monday the whole establishment was working as if nothing bad happened. A large number of men were engaged clearing away the debris, and the large amount of broken metal to be seen on all hands gave the visitor an idea of the havoc which had been made by the fire. The offices, though not destroyed, were not in a fit condition for occupation, and the clerks are carrying on their duties in the Salvation Army Barracks and a portion of what is known as Burlington House. Mr. Richmond, managing direc- tor, received a telegram on Sunday, and came up to Warrington at once to superintend the arrange- ments necessary. Business has been conducted as usual during the week. The firm have made arrangements, with the aid of their new works at Stratford. to keep up their deliveries as usual, and customers have suffered no inconvenience. The buildings which were destroyed by fire were insured in the" Royal "and " Palatine " Assurance Socie- ties, and the damages are roughly estimated at £20,000.

NORTHERN UNION.

The annual meeting ef this unless. was held on Tuesday at Huddersfield,Mr. VVarren,of Warrington,in the chair. There was a gond attendance of club representatives. The report and balance sheet were taken as read, The former stated that membership now stood at 98. and the season closed with a credit balance of £1525 17s. I.d. The committee had formulated a scheme of professional- ism, and hoped that the representatives would support them in legalising payment of membersoto that it might be made honestly and honourably. The balance shoot elbowed receipte anseenting to £2846 2s. 21.. and a bal. ance in hand of £1465 17e. 1.1. In moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet, the president referred to the difficulties which had attended the formation of the union, and said that now the union had a splendid committee and had not looked behind. Mr. Yates (Swin ton) seconded the reeolution, and it was passed. The meeting then dealt with the scheme the committee had formulated legalising professionalism, and the president moved the adoption of the scheme. He re`ferred to the benefit which would accrue from its adoption. and said that the payment of men as hitherto carried on had re. suited in raising the standard of Rugby football. The committee had determined not to tolerate the loafer,ancl insisted that men should be in employmmt. HP pointe out that once players embrared professionalism they would be debarred from taking part in amateur sports, and he thought they would have to start an athletia as- enciation in connection with the Northern Union, and that they might be able to form a very strong athletic association in combination with the association clubs. Mr. Waller (Brighouse) seconded the adoption of part of the scheme which was taken in sectione. and the whole scheme was passed with very few dissentients.

STRANGE CASE. At the Warrington Police Court on Friday last before the Meyer and other magistrates,Henry llaghton, labourer of 87. Knutsford-road was charged with assaulting Mrs. Bridget B owen, 66, St. Mary-street, Latchford on the llth July. Prisoner pleadel not guilty.—Mr. a. Browne who appeared for the prosecution, said ha thought their worships cyanid consider when they heard the case that a very serious and aggravated assault had been corn. mitted. The complainant was the wile of a retired Police Inspector, and on Monday last sloe had been to some friends and the friends saw her home as far as Bridge Foot. When she got up to the Pin Mill the saw a man sitting down. His head was resting on his hand. She walked on and the man said "good-night." The man followed her. She got to her gate and be caught hold of her. He *truck her and she scratched his face. He then caught hold of her dress and behaved indecently to her. She had been scream- ing and Sergeant Leans came up and followed after prisoner and finally caught him. His client's nose had been badly hurt and was dressed at the Infirmary and three stitches put in. IC they considered the evidence sufficient he would ask them to make it an aggravated assault and infilA the punishment accordingly. Mrs. Bowen bore out her solicitor's statement. She said the prisoner followed her up to her own gate, and said good night to her. She Said" who are you speak- ing to " or something to that effect. He then caught hold of her, and assaulted her as she described. She was struggling with him all the time, and said to him. " what are you tieing ; you do not know who I am." She struggled with him, struck him, and screamed merder. and begged of the neighbours to come to her help. Re then strack her on theface, and she said "t am done." Sergeant Evans came running up and fol- lowed after the man who ran away. He brought him I back and then teelc him to the Police Station. She then. I went to the Infirmary.

Sergeant Evans said he was pegging along Knutsford-road on the night in qaestion. Oa coming by Barry-street he heard screams which sounded like a woman. Ele went in their direction and heard someone say " let me alone you scoundrel" and another scream. He then heard the same voice say "Oh God is there none of the neighbours will corns and take this brats from me." He then got up to Mrs. Bowen's gate where he saw the two struggling. Prisoner ran away and after chasing him in a zig,z tg fashion witness secured him._

Further evidence was given by a neighbour. Mrs. Houghtoi saying that on the following Thursday morn- ing she was ieque.sted to examine airs. Bowen. he found her arms were dreadfully bruised and black marks on her body. Tlv prisoner, when asked to make his statiNnent said. !draftsmen passed and sail "get up good man and come on." He then got up and walked with her. He thought rafrs.Bovven was intoxicated,so he walked with her to see her safe. She then said to him " what are you following me for." Sae th.m fell down and must have cut her nose. Sas scrParnsd out murder which frightened him. She struck him aid scrcbodhiin. The officer came running up and he ran away as he was frightened. By the Chairman : He had never known Mrs. Bowen before. _ _
_ Sergeant Evans, recalled by tho Chairman, said Mrs. Bowen was not drunk, bat bad had some drink. She was able to walk to the Infirmary and Police Station without assistance. _ _
The prlsoner was committed to prison for one month with hard labour.
