JULY 22nd, 1893,

NOTHING has been more in- Compulsion and structive than the decline of Conscience. compulsion with regard to vaccination ever sinee the Royal Commission issued its first report. That decline has taken of I late, however, a most remarkable form. It is re- ceiving the ardent support of the firm believers in vaccination, and that is the most remarkable feature in the whole case. Sir HENRY FOWLER vaaled the secret in his remarks about coinpul- 'ion I laaking martyrs. The believers in vaccine- -I°4 law see that making martyrs is a costly busi- -4"; and that men's consciences are entitled to 1/lOre respect than they have received: The leleatific ev;dence taken by the Commission has done its part in weakening the demand for corn-1 111118km/end in increasing the desire to give eritions and limitations. Hence the change in the attitude of the Government and in the public ramd. The non-compulsionists are now a very mixed body. There are persons who object to compulsion because they do not believe in the efficacy of vaccination at all. Others think that the law must respect the views of parents who Object te vaccination in consequence of real or im- aginary risks. The third and larger party, which 1:low includes,as Sir Walter Foster said,the majority 0_ f medical men, object to compulsion because they bt.ellave that its absence will lead to more vaccine- Bolen; to the dying away of agitation on the per- dial rights theory, and to the cessation of martyr- Which influence minds incapable of forming 41111 Y clear judgment whilst their passions are ex- cited. Our own position is largely with this third Class. We concede that the parents who believe that their children are injured by vaccination are entitled to escape penalties. It is of little use endeavouring to silence them by coercion. Rvidence will do this, but not fuses and imprison- ment. Further, we hold that the two theories Will operate side by side much better under a freer system. The non-vaccinating people will have a chance of showing, by a larger body of evidence, whether they can escape contagion and 'hew a larger percentage of recoveries and the like The vaccinated children will always form the larger part of the community, and the effect upon their general health, and their immunity or other- Wise in the midst of epidemics, will become more demonstrable. There will be some severe out-
we ma, better. that in very

breaks, we cannot doubt, and then sciencs will be able tocoinmand attention. The need for what amount of protection vaccination affords will become more urgent, in many minds, when there is no general compulsion. Carelessness may diminish. The attitude of the present re- rannstrants may change. Medical science may riaa: k° new diseoveries. Bacteriological studies are use reasing every year, and their tendency is diB- - favourable to the general theory on which ,accination is based. The use of calf-lympli,more e4re in vaccination, the operations at home, and th• greater calmness of the public mind, will all "-operate to make vaccinations more succe3sful. lu a few years it may be unnecessary to argue the question of vaccination at all. Demonstrations tnay occur to prove its efficacy in some striking fashion. It is conceivable, thcrigh not probable, that its effects may be loss satisfacto •y, and that the operation may be superseded. For these reasons we do not regard the abandonment of even a limited amount of compulsion as inexpedient. We are content to leave the whole matter to the - play of conscience and the demonstrations of science.

Tun course of the war in America's Disenchantment. Cuba has been a succession of disenchantm nits for the Americans. In the first place, they found no in- surgent Government, and nothing resembling an efficient organisation upon which one could be established. In the second place, they discovered the insurgents were of no value as a fighting force. They are now finding that the insurgents are a 1823', plundering, cruel, and incompetent body, for Whena their social and political sympathies are at zero. It is no surprise to us to learn that the insurgents are not to be entrusted with power. They had elected a mayor for Santiago, but he is not to b 3 permitted to take office. The insurgents wanted to loot Santiago, and to wreak their vengeance on the Spaniards. They are now sulking becau3e they cannot have their own way, ;mid in the general opinion of the Am irican soldiers they were not worth fighting for. What is now very probable is that the insurgents may have to be treated as if they were the enemies of order and of humanity. It would be a great mistake to give over to them the control of any part of the surrendered territory. We recognise the difficul- ties in the way of the Americans, and we think President MoKryLty is shewing good sense and humanity in not permitting the insurgent chiefs to have the least control. Were they supreme We believe they would commit crimes which ivtild 4hock the whole of the civilised world. In passing, y remark that the Spaniards have come out of their trials than was expected, and this hour of difficulty, their policy stands little need of defence, as far as their treat-

ment of the insurgents was concerned. As for the refugees, there is less excuse. President Mcli.temav has put the matter very plainly. Ha directs the American Commander to issue a pro- clamation, informing the Cubans that the Americans do not come to make war upon them, but to protect them in their homes, in their em- ployments,in ,their personal and religious rights." Municipal laws are to be respected " as far as compatible with the new condition of things, until suspended or superseded by the occupying belliger- ent." The ports are to be open to the commerce of neutrals. The control of the captured districts will be in American hands until peace is restored. The insurgents will have no power and no authority in civil or military matters. They will not like this submission, but they will have to endure it, and if they become hostile the American Comman- der-in-Chief will make short work of the business. The fear is that insurrection may break out against American authority, either now or at some later stage in the development of events. When the Spaniards have been beaten and they have withdrawn, a plebiscite is to be taken as to the form of Government. The Cubans may be anxious for self-rule, but they will hardly couple with that desire a prayer to be ruled by the insurgents. They would certainly revolt against Garcia and his band, just as Garcia may revolt against any government its which the people of Havana have a preponderating voice. Possibly, the Cubans may desire to be formally annexed to the United States. In any case, we shall, in this country, be content for the Americans to have a free hand, and to do their best for the unhappy island where insurrection has been chronic for so many years.

Dr. W. G. Grace's Jubilee cricket match has after all been played. to a definite finish, and the only cause for the slightest regret in the course of this commemorative contest between Gentlemen and Players is tnat the worthy, burly Doctor has been unable to lead his side to victory. It would have been a fitting triumph to his great career if he could have seen the efforts of himself and his men crowned by succer.Butthis is a matter which had to be left to the disposition of Dame Fortune, who cnose to administer a hard knock to the Gentlemen after thoy had made a gallant Eight. Everything that lay within Vie power of man to accomplish was done, and the 50th birthday of the Grand Old Man of cricket has been celebrated right royally. Quite 50,000 people flocked to the famous Lord's enclosure during the three days of et:s match, and heartily cheered "W. G." on every fitting and possible occasion. The Doctor himself did justice to his great reputation, and if he could not claim the spoils of victory he contributed a couple of characteristsc and invaluable innings to the totals for his team. As a cricketing contest the match was of the highest order, and the magnificent effort by which the Players ultimately triumphed is deserving of a warm approbation which nobody will desire to withhold.

There has been a surprising number of large fires up awl down the country this week, the greatest of which took place at Sunderland and the most interesting,locally of course,in Academy- street, Warrington. The fire at Messrs. Rich- mond's rapidly growing works was short and sharp, but it made a clean sweep -of a newly-erected building used as a warehouse and show-room. The splendid efforts of the fire brigade were successful i I in coping with and subduing the outbreak, so that the greater portion of the establishment escaped I disaster. Beyond the fact that both were fires there is little room for comparison between the blaze here and the devastating conflagration at Sunderland. At the seaport no less than 47 Ibusiness premises were &awn into the fiery vortex, and at one time the area of the blazing property was something like four acres in extent. Sunderland is a town more than twice the size of Warrington, has suffered one of the largest out- breaks of fire in recent years, and is without a fire-brigade One can hardly believe the state- ment. A correspondent says tersely "There is no fire-engine,no fire-brigade, nothing but two officers and a few trained policemen, who have to be taken from ordinary duty." If such an awful state of things as this actually exists in its entirety, then whatever have the Corporation and people of Sunderland been doing When there are 140,000 people without the protection of a fire brigade ex- cept of the most rudimentary description, it is not so surprising that £:250,000 damage can be done by fire in the course of a night. We have indeed something to be thankful for in Warrington. Criticism of our fire-brigade—and there has been not a little of it—should be sunk in feelings of gratification that such an institution is existent in the town. And we must say here that Mr. Turner andhis men tackled the terrifying blaze of Sunday in such a determined and practical way as to limit its demensions to one building in a condensed area That in itself is a feat for which they are deserving. of the highest credit.

Mr. G. F. Chambers, F.R.A.S., writes as follows to the "Times :"—" I notice that, having regard to the fact that the true local times of actual sun- set (and sunrise, of course) differ in different parts of England with differences of latitude and longi- tude,various beaches of magistrates have accepted as a defence when cyclists have been summoned for "no lamp lighted" the plea that the sun had not actually set at the place where the offence was committed by so long an interval as the almanac implied. The plea is more creditable to the smartness of the cyclist than to the legal knowledge of the worthies sitting on the bench. The statute 43 and 44 Viet., c. 9, precisely meets the difficulty. It is called the Statutes (Defini- tion of Time) Act, 1880, and provides that when- ever any expression of time occurs in any Act of Parliament, deed, or other legal instrument, the time referred to shall, unless it is otherwise speci- fically stated, be held in. the case of Groat Britain to be Greenwich mean time,and in the:case of Ire- land Dublin mean time.Presumablylthis enactment was not known to the magistrates at Altrincham, Market Weighton, and their clerks,when they recently dismissed police complaints against cyclists for not having lighted up at the proper time."—Mr. Chambers has, we think, missed the point in a . curious way, and his strictures on magisterial ignorance make rather amusing reading. Toe point is this. Cyclists are required to light up within an hour after sunset, and within an hour before sunrise, but not, as Mr. Chambers seems to imply, at any given hour. If the Act stated that lamps must be lighted at, for instance, 9 p.m., then 9 p.m., would be Greenwich time, but naturally, it does not, as the same time would not do all the year round. Mr. Chambers admits the difference in the hours of sunset and sunrise according to the difference in latitude and longitude, and then quotes the statute defining time, unless otherwise stated, as Greenwich time. This is whero the illogi- cal nature of his argument is apparent. It will be quite clear that the time for lighting up could not be determined by the time of sunset or sunrise at Greenwich. The difference between the times of that event there and here is considerable, though time itself varies only to the extent of a few seconds. Statute 43 and 44 vict. c. 9., does not "precisely meet the difficulty." It has no appli- cation to it whatever. The lighting-up time is only determinable by the hour of sunset and sunrise in each and every locality, and is not affectbd by Greenwich time.

The successful Band of Hope Festival in connec- tion with the Lancashire and Cheshire Union which was held in Parr Hall last week should help to stimulate and encourage the local Band of Hope workers to further efforts. The consolida- tion of the socioties in Warrington and district into one Union has aroused additional interest in Band of Hope work in the town but it is to be hoped that the Union will not be content to let its usefulness end at large public gatherings. The really effective work must be done in the Band of Hope societies themselves, and at the conference

which was held last Saturday afternoon some ad- mirable suggestions were made for conducting Band of Hope Work and extending the usefulness of the societies. Several vigorous speeches were delivered at the eveninc, meeting,and from the re- marks of the Rev. H. J. Taylor of Southport it will be seen that he takes a very sanguine view— too sanguine many will think—of the early victory of the Temperance Cause and the over- throw of the drink interests. The Rev. Canon Hicks referred at some length to the leakage from the Band of Hope societies, and suggested as remedies that the older members should be drafted into the great temperance benefit societies,and also that there should be more pre- cision in the teaching at Band of Hope meetings. This is a point very often overlooked by temper- ance people. It is almost useless to be continu- ally indulging in opprobrious epithets against the drink traffic and all its works. The children must be clearly shown the many advantages of tem- perance, and so instructed as to be able to intelli- gently defend the position they have taken up.

The agitation which has been set going by the " Daily Chronicle" with reference to Vie sufferings of the white-lead workers in the Potteries, is net only jastified but appears likely to bear good fruit. In the House of Commens last Thursday, Mr. Drage asked the Home Secretary for statistics showing the , effect of the dangerous employment in the Pot- teries on the health of the workers. The reply Iproves the evil effects of lead-poisoning to be really startling in their frequency. Said the Home Secretary.—" The total number of recorded cases of lead-poisoning among wore3n and girls engaged in the manufacture of earthenware and china dur- ing the two and a half years since the Act of 1895 came into force is :—Women 528, girls 63—a yearly average of about 230. This is out of a total of 20,700 employed, or to put the case in plainer terms,one in every forty has been affected. These statistics relate to the number of reported cases, and when we consider how many cases had probably escaped being recorded, the roll of death and disease assumes an lappalling aspect. Some of the revelations which have, and are still being made in the capital of the horrors of lead poisoning and phossy-jaw make us wonder seriously whether the Factory Act and Employer's Liability Bill really are efficacious. There. is a screw loose somewhere, and this appears to be in the non-restriction of the use of injurious forms of lead. Expert evidence has shown that these dangerous substances cou:d be dispensed with to a very great extent,and the only reason why they are still extensively used is that the Compensation Act does not give the victims the redress they de- serve. Until the use of this poisonous lead is prohibited bylaw, or the Compensation Act is so extended as to give the suffering employes a hold on their masters, lead-poisoning and its kindred horrors will continue to be attached to the condi- tions of employment of some 20,000 people in the Potteries.

The statement that there are, at most, only eight fully efficient gunners in the Channel squadron demands, if true, a searching investigation into the position and prospects of this important branch of the naval service. The naval lessons drawn from the Battle of Santiago are pregnant with moaning for this country. If our gun power is bad our costly ships will not avail us in the day of trial. At this juncture it is particularly important that the navy should be ready for active service down to the last button. The exaiso of the British Admiralty that the manceuvres could not take place owing to the lack of sufficient coal has practically been dropped. The Channel squadron is going eight hundred miles north. That will not save much coal, and it is significant that .the programme has been so designed that the ships are practically always in touch with the Admiralty offices. Russia has also dropped her naval manoeuvres, because she has only 50,000 tons of coal—a toler- able supply—in store, and these may be required "in certain eventualities:" This mutual disposi- tionon the part of the British and Russian autho- rities to shrink from sending their warships very far from home is decidedly curious, and past his- tory teaches us that such portents may not lightly be disregarded when it is a question of readiness and efficiency. At this juncture, with statements afloat reflecting upon the efficiency of British gunners, the public cannot fail to be per- turbed to some extent, and an oflhial statement would be welcome and, it is to b 3 hoped, reassur- ing.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF A FORMER RUNCORNIAN AT ANNAN.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF A FORMER RUNCORNIAN AT ANNAN.

The" moan Observer "contains the following report of the wedding which took place on Tuesday, the 12inst. at the U. P. Chnrch, Annan, Scotland, of Miss Ellen Scott Robinson, third daughter of Mr. H. Robinson, of The Cereals, with Mr. William Konnan, formerly teacher at the Runcorn Board Schools. The weather was fine, and there was a large assemblage, mostly composed of ladies, whose gay summer costumes gave quite a festive appearance to the event. The pulpit and stairs, by the wish of Nix'. and Mrs. Robinson, were quietly decorated by Mr. James Rae with palms, aspidistras, and ferns, in keeping with the simple though impressive proceed- ings throughout. The hour fixed for the marriage was two o'clock, but quite an hour before that time the con- gregation began to arrive with the object of viewing the ceremony from the most advantageous position.' and when the bridal party entered there wad scarcely an empty seat in the body of the church while many were accommodated in the gallery' As the visitors were assembling„ Miss Johnstone played Wagner's Wedding March from " Lohengrita." Ten minutes before the hour the bridegroom arrived, accorn- panied a. best man by his younger brother, Mr. John Konnan. While the congregation were singing the hymn, The voice that breathed o'er Eden," the bridal party entered,the bride hauling on the arm of her father, who subsevently gave her away. She wore a dress and train composed ontir,ly of rich Ivory moile velours silk, the bodice being very tamefully tucked with ivory chiffon aad trimmed with Brussels lace,the train having a ruche of tucked chiffon. The veil was of embroidered chiffon,aud the '.ouq.let of whit rosesorange blossoms, &-. The bridesmaids were Miss Bey Robinson,younger sister,and Misses Jessie and Janie Rohinson,nieces. Min ' Betsy Robinson wore a beautiful ivory silk bengaline, the bodice being tucked with itself and trimmed with , ivory chiffon, with a long tuck of silk. Her hat was a 1 Napoleon-shaped taque,with chiffon and ostrich plumes. The little nieces were very simply and tastefully dressed in liberty saes of heliotrope satln, trimmed with accordion-pleated white chiffon. "fh,y carried baskets of flowers, and wore picture hats with ostrich plumes. Th bricle wore a pendant and the bridesmtids gold bracelets, the gifts of the bride- groom. The Rev. James Ronald, the officiating minis- ter, having made the preliminary declarations, engaged in prayer. This was fniltliVrYi by an exhortation to the betrothed, after which the vows were imposed. There- after Psalm cxxxviii. was sung, and the prayer having again been offered 2nd Paraphrase was rendered. The Rev. Mr. Ronald then pronounced the Benediction after which the bridal party signed the registration schedule. As they left the church, Miss Johnstone played Mendel- ssoho's " Wedding March." Afterwards an" At Home" was held at Toe Cereal., where the guests had an oppor- tunity of viewing the wedding presents, which were numerous and handsome. Congratulations and best wishes for their future welfare and prosperity were offered to the newly-married couple, who left by the 5.13 train for the Lake District, where they are to spend their honeymoon. Mrs. Kennan's travelling dress was of navy Amazon cloth, the bodice and sleeves tieing braided all over and the bodice trimmed with silk and velvet. She also wore a fawn sac coat.

WITKINS-AIREY.

There was a numerous and fashionable assem- blage at St. Peter's Church, Newtomon Wednesday afternoon on the occasion of the marriage of Mr. gdwin Cecil Watkins, fourth son of Dr. J• W. Watkins, Stoueleigh, Newton, to Annie Beatrice, eldest daughter of Mr. George Aire), of Sandfield Hall, Newton-le-Willows, of the firm of Airey and Sons. Victoria Breweries, Wigan. In consequent if both families being particularly well known and highly respected, coasiderable interest was centred in the affair, and as a consequence all the approaches to the church were crowded with people anxious to obtain a glimpse of the wedding party, and particularly of the bride, who has been a prominent member of the Newton-le-Willows Orchestral Society. From the outer gate red closh was laid to the front entrance of the church, and small streamers were hung at intervals, which en- livened the aspect of the church yard. Inside the church the scence was a brilliant one, the varied colours of the ladies dresses, making a picture as charming as it was kaliedoscopic in character. The chancel and choir stalls had been beautifully de- corated with a profusion of choice flowers and rare plans, the design showing great artistic taste, fbr which every credit is due to Mr. Jackson, gardener, at Brookside, Newton. Mr. P. H. Crossley,tof War- rington and Liverpool, presided at the organ, and during the interval of waiting for the wedding party, played Lohengrin'a "Bridal March." The service was fully choral, and as the bride entered the church on the arm of her father, the choir sang "Toe voice that breathed o'er Eden." The brides- maids were the Misses Ada, Mabel, Letty and Connie Airey (sisters of the bride) and Miss , Beatrice Watkins (sister of the bridegroom)awaited the coming of the bride, on each aide of the aisle and as she passed along, they fell in and followed her to the chancel steps, where she was joined by the bridegroom, and his best man, Dr. Harold E. Watkins. The bride looked very pretty and becom- jag in a dress of rich ivory white duchesse satin, with deep flbunce on new skirt outlined with chiff m ruches and traits of orange blossom. The train was elegantly draped from the shoulder and fastened at the waist with a handsome buckle, both corsage and train being daintily trimmed with chiffon and sprays of erange blossoms. She wore a coronet of orange blossom and Limerick lace veil caught up with two diamond crescents, and carried a lovely bouquet of white exotics,the gift of the bridegroom. The costumes of the bridesmaids consisted of white soie de chine slips, charmingly trimmed with in- sertion and frills of lace,worn over apple green silk skirts, bodices en suite. The remaining two bridesmaids wore pale pink rose toques veiled with lace and carried bouquets of roses to match. Two cases rcsulting from the Warrington harm and cattle fair were heard at the Borough Court on Wednes- day,before Mr. John Faircictigh (in the chair), and other magistrates. The first case was that in which John Ryan Kay-street, Dundalk, was charged with cruelly illtreat- ing a bay mare in the fair ground on Tuesday.—P.C. Clough said the prisoner was given into his custody on Tuesday afternoon by In.pector Greatrex for illtreating a bay mare. Tite animal was attacbcd to a trap, and had several loag whip marks on its body.—lnspectar Oreatrea said that at 2-30 on Tuesday he saw prisoner elriving a bay mare in the fair ground. Be was heating it severely with a stick, and it had marks two feet lung on each side at the body. It was in a poor cor.iition and was lame on the hind legs. ' On Monday he saw the horse, trap, and harness put up for auction, and the best bid was El 10i. for the lot.—The magistrates fined prisoner lOs and costs 143 6d.— In the second case John Bond, cattle dealer, of Belfast, I was charged vrith being drunk in charge of a horse in the fair ground at 3 45 on Tuesday afternoom,and further charged with cruelly working and beating the animal. , —P.C. Chrimes said be saw Bond,who was drunk, rack-: lessly riding a chestnut mare about tin fair. He wa.. acting like a wild man to the danger of the public.—la-1 spector Lue.kings, R.S.P.C. A., said he saw Bond un- mercifully beating the animal. Fie told him to get off and tie it up. Bond was drunk. He afterwards got en 11 the horse again, but was oulled off by earns men, who took his ‘a hip away from him. He, however, gat on again. He knocked a hula child down, and hit a man across the face with a whip. The animal's mouth w raw and bleeding. On the way to the Police Station ho threw himself on the ground and used filthy language.— Bond was fined 55., and costs for being drunk, and 203., or one month's imprisonment, for the other offence.

CROSS Stratmw s FOR ASSAULT —This was a Cross summons between Mary Dacall, 9, Carlisle-street, and Minor Ban- croft, 14. Carlisle-street. The assaults were alleged to have taken place on the 9tri July.—Mrs. B mcroft said on Saturday night about 8 o'clock her husband was sitting on the doorstep and she was in the hou e when Mary Caspian came across the street. Some dispute had arisen about the children and a dog. Mary Dagnall scratched her face and struck her. Her evidence was corroborated by her husband Mr. Bancroft and a Mrs Birchall.—Mi:e Mary Dagnall rutve evidence as to going across the street to speak to Mrs. Bancroft. Mrs. Ban- croft said ''get ayfay you street-walker" and knocked her away. Her evidence was corroborated by two other witnesses. After considering the case the bench fined Mrs. Bancroft the Costs and dismissed the other case. SATURDIY.—Before Mr. J. W. Hayward (in the chair) and ' Mr. R. T. Fairclough. A BEGGIRO IQUISANCE John Harrison of no fixed abode was charged with b.gging in Horsema ket-street at ten minutes past eleven on Friday morning.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—P.O. Edwards said he saw the prisoner drunk and begging in Horsemarket-street. A g ntletnan having refused to give him money the prisoner used foul language to him. Witness cautioned him, and he began begging in Winwick-road, and threatened one gentlAnan because he re- fused to give him money —P.O Sharpe said he received com- plaints about prisoner going horn shop to shop begging, aed using filthy language and threatening people when refused. When prisoner was locked up he behaved disgracefully in the cells.—P, isomer said he was a collier, emp'oyed in the South Wales Colliery, but in 1833, there was a strike, and he was thrown out of work. Its was making his way back to his home in Wigan. The bench committed him to gaol for one month. Viz ALLEGIID ASSAULT AT IlowLey.—ln the case of John Shaw who was in custody on a charge of inflicting grevlous braille harm on Jo•eph Dooley, rn the 9th inst, the chief Constable stated that that case was remanded from th, pre- vious Wednesday, because of the serious condition of Dooley who up to that time had been in an unconscious condition the result of the injury caused by his fall when prisoner struck him• Under those circumstances it had been thought ad- visable to keep Shaw in custody. He was pleased to state that Dooley was now much better and he did not think there was any Particular need to keep Shaw in custody. The case was remanded until July 300, Shaw being allowed out on ball. meNply.—BefOre Mr. T. Birchall (in the chair). Alderman Blackhurst, Councillor Smethur,t, and Mr. 8. Wright. Mr. Pye was busy at the time and asked prisoner to wait a minute. Prisoner stood by the counter where the coat was lying. Mr. Pys turned his back sad prisoner walked out of the shop with the coat under his arm. : Mr. Pya saw that he had gone, and he went after hi m . n save him go into Mr. Green's (toarber) shop, and he followed him and f ound the coat on a form. Mr. Pye told prisoner he had better go with him, and prisoner then used abusive language. He was given into the custody of P.C. Lewis.— Prisoner said he went into the shop to buy a pair of boots. ST. HELENS v. OSSOBNE

On Monday night at the Os street Baths, Mal- cheater, St. Helens met Osborne In the first round of the Northern Counties Championship. The following were the teams wkieh faced each other :—St. Helens: J. Aspinall, J. Bretton and T. Green P. Ripley (captain). J. MavitY: W. E. Miley, and Preston. Osborne : Hamblett, W. Lister and Harris, E. Ribiuson, J. H. Derbyshire, T. Coe, and Phil Lister. St. Helens won the toss and defended the deep end. Ripley sent in a shot fer St. Helens which failed, but Lister getting away from Kiley swain down and scored In the first minute for Osborne. Tricky work on the part of Derbyshire again gave Lister the ball, and he icored a second time. Aspinall having saved in grand style for St. Helens,Coe sent in a third geal for the homesters, and the score at half-time ttlod—Oshorna 3 goals, St. Helens nil. Turn- ing round, St. Helens were again utterly outclassed,Coe adding three more goals for Osbcrne and Derbyshire two. o:borne were victors by 3 goals to nil. The expenditure of the cemetery committee includes the following amounts fr.r burial fees :—To the rector cf Warrington and his cicrk £66 ; the vicar of St. Paula and his clerk £29 15s 81 ; vicar of Holy Trinity and his clerk £l2 10. vicar vicar of St. Barnabas and his clerk £l2 16, 61 ; vicar of St. Peter's and his clerk, £lB 143 44 : vicar .f St Aim's and his cleilc and sexton, £29 9. 61 ; vicar of St. James' rid his clerk and sexton, £l3 Is ;or a total of £lB2 7s. The wages of the regis- trar and gardeners, total up to £49693 7d ; and the cost of painting at the cemetery has been £2B. On the side of ,",-,me ,he tees received by the Registrar amount to £1,119 16 7.1, and the church burial fees £194 121.

TOWN HALL, PARK AND BATHS. In the ToWu Hall neparttnent a further sum of £l6O has been paid for alterations at Bank Rouse, and to this must be added £339 143 31, for fittings and furniture. T There are also several items of expenditure in connec- tion with the Mayor's parlour ; the decorations cost £47 63 93, fittings and furniture £l9l 17s 9.1 and pictures and ornaments £3O 53 61. The income of this department, apart of course from the rates, consist en. tirelv of rents from other departments, amounting to £195. In connectien with the park the wages of gardeners labourers, etc, absorb £521 163. Trees, plants, and seeds cost £27 43 91; corn and bird seed £4O us 2cl and anew 'shelter £5O 123; the amount of contributiens to the bands £6O. The to-al expenditure in connection with the baths is £931 23 Id ; and 488 33 81 has been received from bathers and £3 133 ed for the use of the baths for galas. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE, GYMNASIUM, ETC. The only item under the receipts of the school attend- ance department is £l2 123 61 paid by parents for the maintenance of children at blind and deaf schools. The salaries of toe Inspector and assistants are at the rate of £llO, £97 10, £B4 103. respectively and there is also a further item of £23 163 for a clerk. In addition a sum of £8 has been paid ea an allowance for overtime. Then there is £ll7 53 9.1 for the mtintenance l.f boys at Industrial Schools ; £165 Is. 81. for ths maintenance of biind and deaf clvldren ; £3O as a contribution to the ship " Clio," and £lO for the ex• penses of the deputation which delivers it. In the analyst's department £27 163 7.1 is received from the Lancashire Coimi-v Council under the Sale of Food and ! Drugs Act ; £67 8a 5118 expended. In the Contagious Diseases (Animals') Department £l4 7s 41 is received from the Lancashire County Council and £lO us 61 is expended, thus leaving a small balance. The Rivers Department has spent £B7 63 7.1, chiFily for surveying the river. There is an item of £5 53 91 far expenses of deputation to Manchester S.AvAge Works. The income of the gymnsitirn has been £lO2 us 41 and the expen- diture £270 84 41. It will the:afore be seen that the gymnasium has cost the ratepayers oa a year's working over £l6O. FINANCE AND GENERAL PUIIPOSES.—COST OF DEPUTATIONS.

The expenditure of the finance department includes £5OO the salary for a year tope noes Fairolough,mayor. The salaries in the town clerk's office amounted to £977 7a 6 and the Borough Treasurer's and Gait:oor3 offices £llB2 193. 101.•' and toe Borough Surveyor's office £765 64. 83; and £5OO 11. B. White, clerk to the Borough Justices. £lOBO has been paid to the Museum and Library Fund as the proceeds of a rate of 14 in the R.. The expewes of the deputations to London, re Treasurer' Institute, Local Government Board &0., amounted to £9 74. 61, Bank interest and commission ha e been paid to the ex- tent of £244 13s. 101 other items include £350 for a year's instalment of cost of obtaining provisional order 1896 and interest ; £46 Os. 33. for deficiency of Borough rate due to differential rating in the townships of Little Sankey and Poulton under the Warriagton Extension Order 1896; and £99 5% 51. for similar purpose in the township of Latchford. In the General Purposes de- partment the charges of Parliamentary agents are set forth as follows :—re Mersey Docks and Harbour Board £29 93. 41; re Manchester Corporation Bill, £45 lls. 93; £5O was required by the Board of Trade as a deposit fee re electric lighting; and the advertising of the same cost £26. Deputations to London re Municipal Corporations Association have cost £B5 Sc. 61., and the expenses of the deputation to Preston re the widening of Warrington Bridge were £4 12s 9L The expenses re the opposition to the Manchester Cor- poration sewage scheme were £2O. The Jubilee address to Her Majesty the Queen cost the ratepayers ten guineas, and the caskets and scrolls for Freemen of the Borough £2ll ss. div.head: HOSPITAL AND HEALTH DEPARTMENTS.
div.p: HOSPITAL AND HEALTH DEPARTMENTS.

_ The income of the hospital department amounts to £371 2s and the expenditure to £1,875 13s 6d. The in- come is mainly due to the payments of the Newton Urban District Council and the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council for the use of the hospital and the main- tenance of patients. The expenditure includes £165 14s 2d for the medical superintendent's salary, £339 149 7d for matron's, nurses', and servants' wages, and £437 15s led for provisions. The income of the health department is £5 4s 91 and the expenditure £829 2s 31. which includes expenses of deputation to Manchester Sewage Works £5 5s 9d,to various towns re abattoirs £8 16s 91, expenses of Borough Surveyor and Medical Officer of Health rit Sankey Brook £3 12s ed.

div.p: SANITARY WORKS.

Taking the net cost of work- ing the sanitary works department including the Long. ford and intercepting depots ; and night soil collection it appeArs irom the reLurn that it has cost the ratepayers £7,560 3s.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO A. LOCAL CRICKETER.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO A. LOCAL CRICKETER.

On Saturday afternoon immediately after the match between the Sankey Wire Mills and the Cheshire Lines Engineers, a marble timepiece was presented to Mr. 11. Cooke,the wicket keeper of the Wire Mills' teem. The presentation had been con- tributed by the members of his club,on the occasion of his recent marriage.

TEDLP&RANCE HALL. At the weekly meeting of the Good Templars of Latchford on Monday evening. Bro. Councillor Ellison occupied the chair. A abort debate took place on the working of the order by BrosTearson, Fletcher, Richardson and H.Blease. Bros.A. Hemp- eon, G. Jones and H. Fletcher, gave interesting ex- periences of their ramble last lodge night. Bro. A. Ford gave an excellent address on the subject " Country versus Town." A LOCAL CHARACTER IN TROUBLE AT NOUTHWICH.

At the North wich Police Court on Monday morn- ing, before Messrs. Weston and Cliff and Dr. More- ton, Michael Dowd, labourer, was charged with having been drunk ane disorderly in Church-street, Northwich, on Sunday. Constable Dolan met him coming out of a lodging-house. He was very drunk and disorderly. It was stated that defendant had been convicted five times for drunkenness at North- wich, and 27 times at Warrington. The Bench im- posed a fine of 10s and 5s 8d costs, with the alter- native of 14 days' imprisonment. PRESENTATION AT THE PARISH CHURCH.

An interesting presentation took place at the Parish Church on Friday evening, after the usual choir practice, when Mr. W. Dennett, one of the members of the choir, was presented with a hand- some marble timepiece,on the occasion of his mar- riage. The Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis),in mak- ing the presentation,spoke very highly of Mr. Den- nett' s services in the choir, and in various other branches of parish work. Mr. Dennett made a suitable reply. The timepiece was on view in Mes.rs. Woods's window, Corporation-street, on liaturday. THE SALVATION AWAY_ BARRACKS.

The Sa.l.;;;ti-o-ti- Army Barracks, Academy-street were re-opened on Saturday afternoon after alter- atious and renovation. Ante-room i have been con- structed for the holding of minor meetings, or for offices &c. The hall has been well ventilated, and the walls and ceiling have been decorated. The accomodation for worshippers has also been in- creased. The meeting on Saturday was largely attended, and afterwards over 100 sat down to tea. Colonel Eady, of Manchester, end Major Chantler,of Liverpool,conducted the meetings during the week- end.

div.head: LATE DIRS. CAVANAGH.
div.p: THE LATE DIRS. CAVANAGH.

Alluding to the late Mrs. the " Catholic Times " says :—" By the death of Mrs. Cavanagh, wife of Mr. G. J. Cavanagh, newsagent and bookseller, of II orsemarket-street, Warrington, the poor have lost a true friend. The deceased lady was of a very obliging and genial disposition, and was greatly esteemed by all with whom she came in concoct. She was the poor persons' friend, and very willingly helped deserving cages. During the coal strike of 1893 Mrs. Cavanagh did not forget those who were in consequence of the strike thrown on the verge of starvation. She visited many houses and did much more in this human and praiseworthy cause than many people imagined. It had been truly said of her that she would willingly sacrifice all she had in order to relieve those who were in want. Not only did she give pecuniary assistance, but she also endeavoured by her r. (1 vice to lift them to a step higher in the social ladder of perfection. Mr. Cavanagh has received letters from all parts of the country, including many from the colleges, from priests who knew the deceased lady, condoling with him and his family in the sad loss they and the poor people of Warrington had sustained.

THE LATE MR. JAMES ENGLAND. Dar air,—illow me to thank you for the short a:"- c)unt you gave,irt last Saturday's 'Baal of your pmper,if the life of my late lather, which was to thos i of us who were closely relmted to him, interesting reading. There is, however, I find a slight error which I take the oppor- tunity of correcting. It states in the account that his father and his brother both died suddenly. So far ss the brother was concerned this was correct but not sie in the case of the father as he did not die until after passing through a lingering illness. I might also add that although my late father avra at one time as you state manager at Messrs. Robinson and Bolton's glassworks,he was first of all an ordinary workman there. I simply mention this in honour of my late father's memery,as be was one of those who was never ashamed of being described as a workingman believing that in all honest labour there is truo dignity."—Tours truly, E. ENGLAND. Moss House, Stockton Heath.

"UNROMANTIC AND sLovENLr REMNANTS." Sir,—Can you find space far a few words of kindly remonstrance ? All of us who are fortunate enough to live is the c3untry are, I trust, glad to see people walk- ing out, and enjoying themselves, but, nevertheless, we cannot help wishing that they were not so liberal in distributing their waste, often greasy paper, which gives an udtidy and certainly slumlike air to our fields and gardens. Nat to speak of myself, though almost every morning I find thess unpleasant relics I was yesterday parsing tbrotrzh the beautiful dingle at Appleton, and was sarry to notice something like a dozen greasy sheets of newspaper on the grass in a circle, evidently the makeshift table-cloths of a luncheon, or tea party, with the debris of the feast. The offenders would probably have been the first to complain, had others lett for there such unromantic and slovanly romnants in this leafy glade !—Yours, kc., ROBERT DAVIE% July 14, Mi.

div.head: PLUMBERS' STRIKE.
div.p: THE PLUMBERS' STRIKE.

Sire—For the past three weeks the plumbers of War- rington have been on strike, and to avoid any misunder- standing the Masters think ic only right that the publio should be informed what the strike is about.

. - The working rules in forc•, which were agreed upon by both the mestere and employees, allowed 41 per hour and time and a half from 530 to 7-30. Lately however, the men have drawn up a new set of working rules, in which they demand an advance of 11 per hour which would make their wages 91 per hour or £2 Os 61. wr week of 54 hours. The meters although refusing to grant the advance asked for, have nevertheless offered to inereass the rate of wages to 611 per hour or 3s 31 per week of 54 hours. We consider thia a very fair wage, especially in view of the fact that the Amalgama- ted Society of Pmeabers allow members of their society to work for railway companies and manufacturing firms at a much less rata of wages than we are compelled to pay in our shops. What chance then. can the masters have of securing any orders for work from any of these firms, so long as the Workmen's S )ciety allow their members to do this ? We understand that two shape in the town have given the advance asked for but we wish to draw attention to the fact that they do not belong to the Masters' Feieration,and we are more. over informed, do all their work themselves and do not employ any outside labour. We appeal to the public to assist us in our legitimate refusal to comply with the men's unreasonable demands, by holding back if toes- Bible any work they may have to do until a settlement takes place. We have held several meetings and tried to show the men how difficult along with our increased liability as masters it is to find work at the preseat rate charged by the masters which is 101 per hour, and pointed out to them that if their demand for an increase to 9d. per hour was granted, the masters would be in the position of keeping open a shop for a profit of I.d. per hour per man. Truly a magnificent profit out of which to pay rent, rates and taxes, as and water and other necessary expenses. . . .

In conclusion' We'beg to state that all ths misters who are members of the Masters' Federation are 1.111121.01M1114 in their refusal to give any more than thy have already offered to tbe men. Signed, MASFERS PLUMBERS ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON Ciiit.M.BFAR, OF COHNIRRCE. Dear sir,—Referriag to your report of the procvdings of the Chamber of Commerce,' shall he glad if you would allow me to set forth at sotnewhat greater length the ideas that have occurred with ugard to ittcreaung the usefulness of the present Chamber. . .

The membership at present is confined to about 40 representative.; of manufacturers in Warring79n. It is felt that the number ought to he increased to three hundred and that a cordial invitation be extended to bankers, solicit.u.s,professional men and general traders, to join the Chamber. It is proposed to set apart one room for newspapers, illustrated and otherwise, another room for samples of the manufacturers carried an in the town, and a third room for general news with the latest cables and tele- grams and where members could meet during the day. The subscription is one guinea per annum and tn.rn. bees would have the privilege of introducing a friend to the Chamber. . . . .

I Intending members should communicate with tho Secretary, Mr. Arthur Bennett, Market Gate Chambers. Should an adequate response be made to this appeal, suitable premises would be at once engaged in the centre of the town to carry out the proposed work.— Yours faithfully, E. L. FLEMING.

div.head: RE PLUIIBERS' STRIKE.
div.p: RE PLUIIBERS' STRIKE.

Dear Sin—ln last Saturday's edition of the“Obse.rver" appeared a letter from the Master Piumbers Association of Warrington. This letter is misleading to the general public, as it contains very little of the true facts of the case in it. First of all our Rules are not signed by the Master Plumber's Association at all, we have none nor ever had any with them. The Rules of 1894 belong to the Master Builders' Assoeiation. Further, we have never had time and a half, nor have we asked for it, from 530 to 730 p.m. They next go on to mention about a new set of Rules that we submitted. We wish to sheer the public what is true in this respect, viz. :—The Master Plumbers on our first meeting with them offered us al9 hours week, summer and winter, at the rate of 8 I per hour ;no extra time for overtime from 5-30 to 7-30. This me ait a reduction on our old rate of wages of 23 53 per week along with some of the most redictilous rules as to who a man should work for, have half an hour for his dinner in yrinter,etc. We then drew up a set of rules differing from the roles of 1994 very slightly, the greatest item being the I per hour advance. The Master Plumbers agreed to these rules with the exception of the I per hour advance offering us in place thereof I. We proffered to settle the dispute at id per hour all the year round. This they would not concede, although oth3r trades have had this advance without the need of a strike. Their reasons for not being able to give more, being the price of brass and the Employer's Liability Bill. Thus a respectable tradesman is looked upon in the light of a fluctuating market commodity, and the Employer's Liability Bile being a law of the realm happens to apply to other trades, as well as the plumbing ; more flimsy arguments for keeping down wages it would bee difficult task to find. Again we were compelled to draw our membere from the builders' shope, and these gentlemen, the master builders, only got 7 (lave of a notice, where the master plumbers got 7 months of a notice. The master builders asked us for a deputationto wait upon them and were surprised at us bringing out our members, and most graciously offered us more monev than we proffered to go in to the other party for, viz. IV summer, 541 hours per week and 91 winter,47 hours per week. On sueh an offer as this our members immediately commenced work again for them. This wage will average for all the year round about 34s 61. per week which can only be considered a fair rate of wages, to men carrying on a skilled trade like plumbing in which men are early incapacitated from the character of their work, from following their calling, and are moreover liable to a great amount of sickness,and a ree of mortality higher than in any other branch of the Building Trades. Again Sir, the men working under private firms are getting an averaee wage greater than the men in .hops, railway men excepted, but these enjoy far more privileges than any man in a shop does. Further these members do not take any work out of the town, nor do the railway companies compete with the oepreesed master plumbers for work in any part of the country. Any ordinary parson will see the demand is only a very fair one, considering the amount of scientific knowledge that a plumber must acquire,to keep himself up to the times in the rapid progress of sanitary work, and especially if he wishes to peeve his qualifications be passing the Graded Examinations for Registration. Again, we as plumbers are only aski-g to be put on the same terms as other skilled tradesmen viz --joiners, and bricklayers, plasterers Stc. and we are determined to hold out for our rights. We winder how many of the readers of th master plumbars' letter considered how many firms there were asking for the work to be kept back ? Perhaps they will be sur- prised when we mention that where our members are employed they can be counted on one hand. We think Mr. Elitor, thit a greater piece of audacity, you cannot call it anything else, could not have been shown, for it not only casts a reflection on the few men who are still out, but it reads as though the Master Builders and other respectable firm, of plumbers who do oot belong to tbe undertaking M" ter pi u mAssociation,b in are not cape work. The whole gist of i heir letter shows nothing but the elfish nature of these firms affiliated with the Masters' Associa- tion. Indeed it seems difillult to understand their action for their own president speakinir at Derby on the 11th May, 3.193 said : "They were not banded tegether to be grasping or tyrannical, but to put the trade on a better footing." Yrt what is this branch doing, trying to out us down under all other trades in the town, and at that they are supp 'Bed to be practical plumbers' Should they come V?w ele again, and there are many nee and downs in iffy., it is to be hoped that the public will hold with them in the poor estimation they have of their I

It was a practical one, and one that could be werkel on the present premises without any 'appreciable expense. If the scheme were adopted and systeneatically and vigorously worked it would lead to recoaemy rather than an increased expen- diture. There were a number of people who had no business at all to be inside the Workhouse, and for whom the place was too geed and too easy. The cost per bead might be increased a little by the proposed claesification scheme, but the gross cost would fall because semi who were now inmates and were being maintained at the expense !of the rate- payers would leave the Workhouse. There were some inmatee,undeserving of any pity or consideration from the Guardians. But there were a few people who were deserving of better treetment than the average inmate, and to these people he thought better treatment ought to be accorded. They were desirous of keeping abreast of the times in the administration of relief. (Hear, hear.) There was another matter which had weighed with him personally in trying to get the classification scheme into working order,and that was the subject of out-relief which was a serious matter. In four years the nut-relief of their Union had gone up 35 per cent. and it was now 40 per cent, above the average amount paid by other unions. The expenditure in out-relief had increased from £3,700 to nearly £5,000 per annum in four years. He submitted that was a serious matter for the consideration of the Guardians. One argument which had been frequently used against sending people into the house Was that it was unfair to make aged, decent, poor people enter the workhouse, to be con- ticuelly in the company of degraded people. The Board would do well to sanetion the proposed scheme of classi- fication because it would remove the grounds which at present eitistel for not strictly adhering to the principle of offering the house to applicants for relief.So far ae the subcommittee had gone the members were unanimous it thrOleeisions arrived at. fie thought that even if the scheme was going to cost the Board more—and he did not think it was—it was deserving of support on finan- cial grounds if it gave them a reasonable means of keep- ing down ow-relief. The scheme had been patiently considered by the committee appointed for the purpose, and althou‘th it wag not entirely an ideal scheme, it was an eminently practical scheme. He did not think it would involve any capital expenditure, but rather on the other hand reduce it, still if it did incur some ex- pense it would be money well-spent in carrying out what w 49 really an improvement in the house. The scheme was a great advance on present methods. Me. THORNTON said personally he felt pleased that the scheme had been brought before the Guardians and carried so far. Even if it cost the livardiana a little more he thought it ought to be carried out, and in the end he believed it would be a saving to the ratepayers. Mr. KNOWLES said the assurance that the scheme was not going tc cost anything extra went a long way with him, and he did not make any eerie) as objection to the scheme. div.p: ANGLICAN ROMANESNI : BAPTISMAL RE(3 EN ERATION.

Sir,—The doctrine named in my heading is a most important article of Faith in the Raman Catholic Church, forming in fact one of the corner stones upon which her religious system is based and maintained. She describes it as"A Sacrament which cleanses us from original sin, makes us Christians, children of Gad, awl members of the church." And, moreover, she tells us that " Baptism also forgives actual sins,with all punish- ment due to them, when it ii received in proper dis- positions by those who have been guilty of actual sin." (Catechism of Christian Doctrine approved by the Cr- dial Archbishop and Bishops of Eagland and Wale..) The identity of thie teaching, with that of the Church of England is so remarkable that we are compelled to conclude that both churches founded it upon the same traditions. But let us amplify a little. _ .

In the twenty-- viseth "'Article of ' Religion " we are informed that 3:19111 is not only a sign of profession, and mark of dilerenee, whereby Christian men are die- corned front others that be not christened, but it is also a sign of regeneration of new birth, whereby, as by an iastrument,they thet receive baptism rightly are grafted into the Church ; the promises of the forgivesiess of sin, and our adoption to be the sons tot God by the Holy Ghost, are visibly signed and sealed." Ordinary mid, kuowing something of the New Testament would natur- ally enough cenclude that the recipient of a rite so me- mentous and far reachiog in its consequences as this, sneuld at least know something about it and be a willing and grateful absentee thereto. But this is evidently not the mind of the Church for, is the artiele from which I have just quoted, we read, " hi Baptiree of infante is in any wise to he retained in the church,as moat agreeable te the institution of Christ." And the ' very age at which the miracle is to be performed upon them is explicitly laid down in the Rubric prefixed to " The Miniscration of Pri•ate Baptism of children in houses." Here is the instruction. " me euratee of every parish shall of too admanish the people, that they defer not the baptism of their children longer than the first or second Sunday next after their birth, or other holy des' falling between, ualess upeo a great and reasonable cause, to he approved by the curate." The baptism commanded by Christ and carried out by his apostles required the exercise of repentance and faith as ab- solutely essential preliminaries, and to this the church very properly assents. But as infants MR neither repeat nor believe she ham invented a method by which the '6 new birth" arid Re accompanying graces can be Me- rarted to them through proxies. When these proxies commonly called godfathers and godmothers, have publicly, in a church or elsewhere, renounced the Devil and all his works, and expressed their belief in what is: called the" Apostles Creed " on behalf of the infants, the Priest says, " We yield thee hearty thanks most merciful Father, that it bath pleased thee te regenerate this infant with Thy holy Spirit,to receive hint for Thine own child by adoption, and to incorporate him into Thy holy church." (Public Baptiern of Infants). Nor is the child himself left long in ignorance of the won- derful change thus wrought upon him by the church. As soon as he is able to learn anything he is taught to regard himself, by virtue of his bapesne, as a member of Christ,the Child of Ged,and en inheritor of the kingdom of heaven." (This Catechism). And yet, strange to sly, thie fine ecclesiastical structure, this positively as- serted regeneretioe is, after all, an imperfect construc- tion. Hitherto the priest has been the priocipel per- former in the miracle ; but it seems that the yoong dis- ciples must feel the touch of a Bishop's hand up in their heads b-fore they can realise all the benefiei of their baptism. But whatever lows there may be in the re- generation process it 1111 St be obvioue, to everyone who ;as studied the suejecr,tleat it is the alpha and omega of the State Ceurch for the salvatioe of men. Ana this view is stronely.coefined by the fact that all baptised and confirmed pereene, who have not teen ex-communi- cate:l nee hie violent handl upon themse'ves, are to ho burled in sure ard certain hope of the resurrectiou to eternal life." (The Burial of the Dead). I pronounce no judeemeet on this extraordinary doc- trine,but content myself be saying that it is either true or false. If true,what a simple and easy method of es- caping the wrath Co come it presents to our tenon race ! If,on the other hand,it is merely an invention of priestly minds, hew tremendous is the responsibility of those teachers who impose it upon the people as an institution emanating from God ! The ritualistic clergy may be Romanisere in small mattere, such as millinery, postur- ing, candles, incense etc., but Baptismal Regeneration is one of the main planks in their platform. And their earnest and consistent advocacy of the doctrine shows that.in this matter at least, they are loyal and devoted eons of the Church by law established.—Yours truly, lONA.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT NEWTON.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT NEWTON.
A SAD STORY.

At the Warrington—C;irn—ty-ie-til Sessions on We dues. day mornirg,betore Mr. John Crosfield and other magis- trates, Edith Janet Smith, a respectably dressed woman of no fixed abode, was charged with unlawfully taking a quantity of laudanum with latest to commit suicide on the 13't July at Newton. Ia reply to tho chsrge prisoner said it was quite corrr

William Richard Knowles, chemist, 59, Market-street, Earlestown, Said tha6 Smith came into his shop on the 13th inst. about 8.30 p.m. She made one purchase,and then asked for an ounce of laudanum. After asking her the usual questions as to what it was for he gave it to her. She told him that the doctor had recemmended it for sleeplessness. In reply to a question by the chair- man witness said laudanum did not appear in the schedule of poisons which had to be registered when sold.

Henry flookee, hooking clerk at Earlestown station, said that on the 12th inst, he went into the ladies' wait- ing-room and found a woman lying down behind the door. He informed the stationmaster, and the police were sent for. She was lifted up by a porter, and a bottle of laudanum fell from her pocket. P.C. Schofield, stationed at Earlestown, said ha was called to the railway station and found prisoner lying unconscious in the ladies' waiting room. He gave her aO emetic, which had the desired effect. A. doctor at- tended her and witness took her to the police etation. He there charged her and she replied " You did not see Inc take it ; there was no one in the roost when I did take it."

_ Prisoner said that all that had been gild was perfeetly correct. Her husband and child had been staying in a S. Helens lodging-heuse,and she had been told they had aurae to Newton races to sell race cards. She went to the course for the purpose of taking the child away from her husband. She did not succeed in finding them, so she came away after the races. She lost her purse and money,and became despondent about the child who was only sewn years old being dragged about the coun- try. Her husband had done no work for some tinse,was not giving him a proper education,and was not bringing her chili up properly. He took the child away one day while she was at work. She had aeon lathe Edinburgh Hoiversity. She be:onged to Dumfries, and her borne had been broken up. She would go anywhere if the police would only try and fiad her little boy. fhe magistrates discharged prisoner on her promising te go to a home, and Mr. Taylor said be would make Inquiries after the boy.

THE FA.TALITY AT A ST. HELENS GLASSWORKS. On Saturlay Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inclupst at St. Helens Town Hall on the body of Samuel Eccleston, 19, years of age, of 46, Corporatipn- Street, who died from injuries received while following his employment as a glass beveller at the plate-glass works of ilossrs. Pilkingtoa Brothers.—Mr. J. 0. Swat appeared for the firm, and Mr. Email:, Government in- spector of factories and workshops also attended.—The Coroner informed the jury that on Monday last Eccles- ton was workiag at a bevelling machine, when, by aroma means, a pad on his apron slipped, and the plate-glass he was working also slipped, with the result that it caught in a nick on the revolving disc. the glass was forced violently back against his stomaoh, and he sus- tained injuries which resulted in his death the following day.—Evidence was given by Alexander Sere, foreman of the bevelling shop, and John Appleton, 13, Hanover• street, a workman, and it was stated that the disc at which Eccleston was working ma le 120 revolutions per noinute.—Appleton said it was Eccleston's anxiety to save the plats of glass which really caused the accident. No such accident had ever occurred at the work. before. —The Coroner said dolt Mr. Eraut had ineed the place, and there was nothims, to complain about. On all the occasions be had dune so he had always find the machinery in good working order.—The jury murned a verdict of "Accidental death."

Joseph Phythian, aged thirty-eight, of Jubilee Cot- tages, Clock Face, St. Helens, received a painful injury on Sunday in the engine-house at the new colliery of the Bold Hall Company. Phythian is engaged to superintend the pumping operations at the mine. On Sunday morn- ing they were testing a new steam cylinder, when the cover flew off, and Phythian was very severely scalded. Dr. Mason was called and ordered the man's removal to the St. Helene Hospital. SHOCKIEG DISCOVERY AT ST. HELENS. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, on the body of the newly-born male child which was found by some boys, on Sunday night,in the front garden of Ravendaie House, Sr. Ann's. Dr. John Masson gave evidence that he had made a post-mortem examination of the bedy,which had Probably been born a week or tea days previously. It was in an advanced state of decomposition. There were no marks or signs of violence externally. The child had probably breathed slightly, and he could not say defi- nitely that the child had a separate existence apart from the mother—The Coroner suegeeted that the jury return a verdict that the child had bsan found—not found dead as that would mean that it had once been alive, but simply found, and that there was no evidence to show whether it had had a separate exieteace.—The jury adopted the coroner's suggestion, and returned a verdict in accordance therewith. FARM FIRE AT CARE. About one o'clock on Monday efcernoon information was received at St. Helens Firs Brigade Station that a fire had broken out on the farm of Councillor John Smith, Newton-road, Carr. The brigade, under Super- intendent Lyon, turned out with the steamer and hose reel, and on their arrival at the spot found a large stack of hay anti an adjoining Dutch barn containing straw in lames. Seine difficulty was experienced in getting a supply of water owing to the situation of the premises, but ultimately the steamer was placed near a pit at Broad Oak, 300 yards away from the fire, and a good supply of water was pumped th,refrorn. In the mean- time the flames had practically destroyed the hay,straws and barn, and the efforts of the brigade were directed towards preventing any further spread. In this they were successful, and the fire was gradually suppressed-. The total loss, which is covered by insurance, is esti- mated at about £2OO. It is not iknown how the fire originated. rEIEFTS FROM • ST. HELENS DRELLINO.MOUSE.

Bernard Clive, a well-dreesed young rntn ,was charged at St. Helens on Monday before Alderman Cook and other magistrates, with stealing £l5, the Property of Albert Hunt, a carter, of 74, Rigby-street. Chief Con- stable Wood said that prisoner came to St. Helens about three weeks ago, and went to reside with Mrs. Rand. of 74, Rigby-street. Hunt also lodged there. Prisoner went into the employ of John Wilson, fruiterer, of Den. ton's Green-lane. He left Wilson's last Thursday, and went back to Rigby street. He disappeared on Saturday morning last, together with a chamois leather bag, con- taining £l5, which had been left by Hunt in his over- coat pocket in his bedroom. On Sunday he was arrested by the Cheshire police at New Brighton, when the hag was found in his possession, containing £l2 Ms 94d. Prisoner admitted taking the money.—The bench sent- enced prisoner, who had been convicted several times,to go to prison for three months' hard labour.

Yesterday Professor Ted Heaton, the champion WO diver and leng-distance swimmer of the world, who 01 appearing at Rhyl this anima, awam from Cal wyn to Rhyl Pier, covering, owing to the currents, a diatanCe of about sixteen miles. He was followed by two beau and a steam launch. He started with the flood tide al 9 a.m, and reached Rhyl Pisr at 1-30, more than an hot% late, the ebb tide having strongly set in. Meekly, Lambert, Ford, Kite, and Roebuck, and W. W. B. Cook (clerk).—The Clerk said that, in accordance with instructions from the previous meeting, he had written to Mr. W. H. Collier, manager of the ship Canal Company, asking if passengers could be allowed to siss the Thelwall terry after nine p.m. at an increased tog up to 84., in acsordanne with the,regolations upon the old notice board. Be received tha following reply "We shall have no objection to the ferry being used after nine p.m. under the same conditions which existed !II the days of the old manor ferry, which were that pee: sons wishing to cross the ferry alter nine p.m. would have to knock the ferryman up and wait until he could ferry them across the canal, the charge being J. eadt person, which charge, as wo do not require the ferryman to work atter nine p en. on the company's account, we purpose allowing him te retain as compensation for his services in working after nine p.m. At the same time, it must be under stood that the company take no risk whatever, aid caw not be responsible for any accident which may arise to persona or property. I may add that our ferryman ha, been in the habit of getting up to ferry persons acroo6 the canal after nine p.m., and being paid extra fare fef doing so."—Mr. Meekly: Were any comments made 00, this question at the last meeting P—The Chairman 550 the question at the last meeting was w.-mther they ouglA to take the risk. If any accident happened after nine p.m. The Ship Canal Company said they would net 1?e responsible.—Mr. Bleckley said that whether the Ship Canal Company repudiated any risk or not, it did net alter the circumstances. If an accident occurred their repudiation would not affect their responsibility in ani way. Re thought it would be advisable to consult s lawyer as to whether they were responsible. If the re. sponsibility did not rest with them anyone who crossed over at night would know it was at their own risk and peril. If the lawyer adviFed them that the Ship Canal Company were responsible, they would only have m t.°, write to the and toll them so.—The Chairman /AP that ne repudiation or risk was mentioned on the cid notice board. If pFople went across at their own risk the company would take them —Mr. Blackly said the company were equally responsible at night-time as 10 the day-time.—After further discussion, it was decided on the motion of Mr. Sleekly, seconded by Mr. Roebuck' that legal opinion be obtained in the matter.—Mt' Sleekly said the inhabitame of the parish should kn9f what po.ition they were in, and it was the Council e duty to lot them know. 411.
